For someone unfamiliar with Kazakh culture, qonaqasy can be explained as the food or meal a host provides to welcome and
honour a guest. It is best understood as a social expression of hospitality rather than as the name of one fixed dish.
sections.Evidence:
●​    “Linguocultural Characteristics of Guest Hosting Traditions of Kazakh and Turkish People.” Research PDF
     ●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: The connection between guest reception, food and hospitality.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic description of qonaqasy as a distinct practice.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; general context identified, but exact pages and specific claims require verification.

heading: ERULIK

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Erulik refers to a welcoming meal or gathering organised for people who have recently moved into a neighbourhood.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Ерулік
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Erulik
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /jeˈɾʊlɪk/
     ●​    Word class: Noun
     ●​    Related forms: Ерулік беру — to hold or provide an erulik; көрші — neighbour.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Erulik refers to a welcoming meal or gathering organised for people who have recently moved into a neighbourhood.

It is particularly associated with the practice of established neighbours inviting newcomers to a meal, helping them become
acquainted with the local community.
sections.Cultural context:
The practice is associated with settlement and neighbourhood relations in traditional Kazakh communities. Moving to a new
place could create a need to establish relationships with surrounding households.

By inviting newcomers to a meal, neighbours helped them become familiar with the community and signalled that they were
welcome.

Although erulik is commonly described as a Kazakh custom, welcoming new neighbours through food and social gatherings
also exists in other cultures. The particular name and customary form are what make this entry relevant to Kazakh cultural
vocabulary.
sections.Social function:
●​   Welcomes newcomers into a neighbourhood.
     ●​   Establishes initial relationships between households.
     ●​   Reduces social distance between new and established residents.
     ●​   Creates opportunities for communication and mutual assistance.
     ●​   Encourages a sense of belonging.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Neighbourliness.
     ●​   Hospitality.
     ●​   Inclusion.
     ●​   Cooperation.
     ●​   Social solidarity.

The practice should not be interpreted as a formal legal or administrative procedure. It is a social custom, and participation may
differ between communities.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Ерулік беру — to organise a welcoming meal for new neighbours.
     ●​   Жаңа көшіп келгендерге ерулік беру — to welcome people who have recently moved in with a meal.

Example: A family moves into a village. Their neighbours invite them for a meal so that everyone can meet and become
acquainted.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Welcome meal for new neighbours: The clearest explanatory equivalent.
     ●​   Neighbourhood welcome gathering: Emphasises the social event.
     ●​   Welcoming feast: Possible when the gathering is substantial, but may exaggerate its scale.
     ●​   Housewarming meal: Not fully equivalent; in English, a housewarming is usually organised by the people who have
          moved.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Erulik is a welcoming meal organised by neighbours for a household that has recently moved into the area. Rather than leaving
newcomers to establish relationships entirely on their own, existing residents invite them to eat and become acquainted.

The practice has a practical social purpose: it helps people recognise one another, begin conversations and establish
relationships that may later develop into mutual assistance. In a close-knit neighbourhood, these relationships can become
important in everyday life.
 The distinction from an English-language housewarming party is important. A housewarming is generally hosted by the people
who have moved into a new home. In the traditional description of erulik, the initiative comes from the neighbours who are
already established in the area.

A suitable explanation is a traditional welcoming meal organised by neighbours for newly arrived residents.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: General discussion of Kazakh customs and social traditions.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic source documenting erulik, its participants and its customary
           sequence.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; the description is a general cultural account, not yet supported by a dedicated page-level
           source.

heading: SYBAGA

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Sybaǵa refers to a portion of food, especially meat, set aside for a particular person or group according to relationship, status, occasion or customary expectation.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Сыбаға
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Sybaǵa
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /sɯˈbɑʁɑ/
     ●​    Word class: Noun
     ●​    Related forms: Сыбаға сақтау — to reserve a portion; сыбағалы ас — food or a portion reserved for someone.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Sybaǵa refers to a portion of food, especially meat, set aside for a particular person or group according to relationship, status,
occasion or customary expectation.

The term is especially associated with the sharing and distribution of meat. It may refer to a portion reserved for an absent
relative, a respected guest or another person who is entitled to receive it within a particular social context.
sections.Cultural context:
The concept is connected with the importance of meat in traditional Kazakh food culture and the social organisation of shared
meals.

In a pastoral society, the slaughtering and distribution of livestock could be significant household and community events.
Different cuts of meat could carry different meanings and be associated with particular guests or relatives.

The precise distribution of portions depended on custom, region, occasion and the relationships between participants. It should
not be presented as one universal and unchanging system.
sections.Social function:
●​    Recognises relationships and social obligations.
     ●​    Expresses respect towards particular individuals.
     ●​    Ensures that absent relatives or expected guests are not forgotten.
     ●​    Organises the distribution of food during important gatherings.
     ●​    Reinforces social bonds through sharing.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​    Respect.
     ●​    Consideration.
     ●​    Family connection.
     ●​    Generosity.
      ●​    Recognition of social relationships.

However, sybaǵa is not simply a synonym for generosity. It may also involve an established expectation that a particular person
should receive a designated portion.
sections.Practical application:
●​    Сыбаға сақтау — to reserve someone's portion.
     ●​    Сыбағасын беру — to give someone their designated share.
     ●​    Сыбағалы ет — meat reserved for someone.

Example: A family prepares meat for a gathering and keeps a particular portion for a relative who cannot attend.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    Reserved portion: The most direct general equivalent.
     ●​    Designated share: Emphasises that the portion belongs to a particular person.
     ●​    Traditional meat portion: Useful when the context specifically concerns meat.
     ●​    Share set aside for a relative or guest: The clearest explanatory translation.

The word serving is too broad because it does not communicate the social expectation behind the reserved portion.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Sybaǵa is a portion of food, particularly meat, that is set aside for someone because of their relationship to the household or
their place in a social occasion. It is not necessarily an ordinary serving distributed randomly among everyone at the table.

For example, when a family prepares meat for a gathering, it may reserve a particular portion for an absent relative or an
expected guest. The act communicates that the person has been remembered and that their relationship with the household is
recognised even if they are not physically present.

The concept therefore connects food with social relationships. It demonstrates how the distribution of food can express respect,
belonging and responsibility.

For an international audience, sybaǵa is best explained as a customary portion of food, especially meat, reserved for a
particular person according to social or family relationships.
sections.Evidence:
●​    “Linguocultural Characteristics of Guest Hosting Traditions of Kazakh and Turkish People.” Research PDF
     ●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: General cultural context of food, hospitality and traditional customs.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A specialist ethnographic source on meat distribution, named cuts and the customary
           allocation of sybaǵa.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; specific ethnographic details and terminology require further verification.

heading: SАРQYT

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Sarqyt refers to food taken home by guests after a meal or gathering, traditionally offered by the hosts.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Сарқыт
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Sarqyt
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /sɑɾˈqɯt/
     ●​    Word class: Noun
     ●​    Related forms: Сарқыт беру — to give someone sarqyt; сарқыт алу — to receive sarqyt.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Sarqyt refers to food taken home by guests after a meal or gathering, traditionally offered by the hosts.
 It is more than simply leftover food. In the customary context, it can represent a continuation of hospitality, allowing guests to
share food from the gathering with family members who were not present.
sections.Cultural context:
The practice is associated with the sharing of food during family celebrations and social gatherings.

In traditional settings, a guest might receive a portion of food to take home. This could allow family members who had not
attended the gathering to share in the occasion.

The practice demonstrates how hospitality can extend beyond the immediate meal and beyond the people physically present.
sections.Social function:
●​    Extends the host's hospitality beyond the gathering.
     ●​    Allows absent family members to share food.
     ●​    Maintains relationships between households.
     ●​    Encourages sharing and remembrance.
     ●​    Gives guests a tangible connection to the occasion.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​    Generosity.
     ●​    Sharing.
     ●​    Family connection.
     ●​    Care for absent relatives.
     ●​    Continuity of hospitality.

It is important not to confuse sarqyt with waste food. The customary meaning concerns food intentionally given to guests, not
merely unwanted leftovers.
sections.Practical application:
●​    Сарқыт беру — to give guests food to take home.
     ●​    Сарқыт алу — to receive food from a gathering.
     ●​    Сарқыт әкелу — to bring home food received at an event.

Example: After a family celebration, the hosts give guests portions of food to take home and share with their families.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    Food given to guests to take home: The most accurate explanatory equivalent.
     ●​    Take-home portion: Concise, but less culturally descriptive.
     ●​    Food shared after a gathering: Emphasises the social practice.
     ●​    Leftovers: Usually misleading because it suggests unwanted or unused food.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Sarqyt is food that guests are given to take home after a meal or celebration. The practice is significant because the food is not
treated merely as something remaining after the event. It is intentionally shared with guests, who may then take it to family
members who could not attend.

This creates a connection between the gathering and the wider family network. A person who was absent can still receive
something from the occasion, and the host's generosity extends beyond the table.

The distinction from ordinary leftovers matters. In English, leftovers usually refers to food that remains after a meal. Sarqyt, in
its customary sense, is better understood as food deliberately offered to guests as an extension of hospitality.

     ●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Supports: General relationship between food-sharing practices and hospitality.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated source explaining the meaning and customary forms of sarqyt.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; specific claims require dedicated ethnographic confirmation.

heading: KÖRIMDIK

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Körimdik refers to a gift or monetary contribution given when someone is presented with something new or significant for the first time.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Көрімдік
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Körimdik
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /køɾɪmˈdɪk/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Көрімдік беру — to give körimdik; көрімдік сұрау — to ask for körimdik.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Körimdik refers to a gift or monetary contribution given when someone is presented with something new or significant for the
first time. It is particularly associated with seeing a newborn baby, a newly married bride or groom, or another important new
arrival or possession.

The word is connected to көру (köru, to see). Its meaning is therefore linked to the act of seeing something for the first time and
responding with a customary gift.
sections.Cultural context:
Körimdik is associated with gift-giving customs in Kazakh family and community life. It can accompany important moments,
especially the arrival of a new child or the introduction of a bride into a household.

The gift may be money or another present. Its form and value depend on the relationship between the people, the occasion and
local practice.

It is important to distinguish körimdik from a general gift: the custom is connected to a particular first encounter or presentation.
sections.Social function:
●​   Welcomes a new person or significant change.
     ●​   Expresses happiness and goodwill.
     ●​   Strengthens relationships between relatives and acquaintances.
     ●​   Allows community members to participate in an important family moment.
     ●​   Creates a customary opportunity for giving.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Generosity.
     ●​   Goodwill.
     ●​   Celebration.
     ●​   Family connection.
     ●​   Participation in important life events.

The practice should not be interpreted as a fixed financial obligation. Expectations differ between families and communities.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Көрімдік беру — to give a customary gift upon seeing something or someone for the first time.
     ●​   Көрімдік сұрау — to ask for the customary gift.
     ●​   Сәбиге көрімдік беру — to give a gift upon seeing a newborn baby.
 Example: Relatives visit a family to see their newborn child and give the baby a small monetary gift.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    First-sight gift: A concise explanatory translation, though not a standard English expression.
     ●​    Welcoming gift: Useful when the custom concerns a newborn or new arrival.
     ●​    Customary congratulatory gift: Emphasises the social occasion.
     ●​    Gift given upon first seeing someone or something: The most precise descriptive equivalent.

It should not be translated simply as tip, because the payment is not compensation for a service.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Körimdik is a customary gift given when someone sees a new person or significant new arrival for the first time. One familiar
example is the gift given to relatives or parents when a newborn baby is introduced to them. The gift may also be associated
with other important first encounters, depending on the custom and context.

The act of giving communicates happiness, goodwill and participation in another person's important moment. It is not primarily a
payment for seeing something. Rather, it is a socially recognised way of responding to a new arrival or event.

For an international audience, körimdik can be explained as a customary congratulatory gift given upon the first presentation of
a newborn or another significant new arrival. The exact occasion should always be specified because the term can be used in
more than one context.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: General discussion of Kazakh customs and family traditions.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic source documenting the different occasions, forms and social
           expectations associated with körimdik.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; the general description requires dedicated source verification.

heading: BASTAŃǴY

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Bastańǵy refers to a traditional gathering or informal celebration, commonly associated with young people meeting at a household when the older members of the family are away.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Бастаңғы
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Bastańǵy
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /bɑsˈtɑŋʁɯ/
     ●​    Word class: Noun
     ●​    Related forms: Бастаңғы жасау — to hold a bastangy; бастаңғыға шақыру — to invite someone to a bastangy.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Bastańǵy refers to a traditional gathering or informal celebration, commonly associated with young people meeting at a
household when the older members of the family are away.

The gathering may involve food, conversation, games, music and social interaction.

Its precise form depends on the household, participants and local interpretation of the custom.
sections.Cultural context:
The practice is commonly described in accounts of traditional Kazakh youth customs. It provided an opportunity for young
people to gather, socialise and spend time together in a familiar domestic setting.

It is sometimes associated with a temporary absence of parents or older household members. However, it should not
automatically be described as an unsupervised or secret party: the circumstances and social expectations could differ.
 A careful cultural account should distinguish historical descriptions of bastańǵy from modern informal gatherings that may use
the same name.
sections.Social function:
●​    Creates opportunities for young people to socialise.
     ●​    Encourages friendships and communication.
     ●​    Provides a setting for games, music and shared meals.
     ●​    Supports informal interaction within a community.
     ●​    Gives young people a degree of social independence.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​    Youth sociability.
     ●​    Friendship.
     ●​    Shared enjoyment.
     ●​    Informal community life.
     ●​    Hospitality.

The concept should not be reduced to a modern house party. Its traditional context and social meaning are important.
sections.Practical application:
●​    Бастаңғы жасау — to organise or hold a bastangy.
     ●​    Бастаңғыға бару — to attend a bastangy.
     ●​    Бастаңғыға шақыру — to invite people to a bastangy.

Example: A group of young people gathers at a family home while the older members of the household are away, sharing food
and spending time together.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    Traditional youth gathering: The most suitable general equivalent.
     ●​    Youth social gathering: Emphasises the participants.
     ●​    Informal house gathering: Describes the setting but loses the cultural specificity.
     ●​    House party: Understandable, but may suggest a modern party with different expectations.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Bastańǵy is a traditional form of youth gathering associated with Kazakh domestic and social life. It is commonly described as
an occasion when young people meet at a home, sometimes while the older members of the household are away. They may
share food, talk, play games, sing or enjoy one another's company.

The important feature is not simply that a party takes place in a house. The term refers to a socially recognised type of
gathering with a particular cultural and generational context.

For an international reader, it can be understood as a traditional informal gathering of young people, often held at a family
home. The explanation should avoid assuming that every gathering followed exactly the same rules or circumstances.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: General discussion of Kazakh customs and social practices.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic or folklore source on bastańǵy, especially its participants,
           setting and historical variations.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; specific historical and social details need further verification.

heading: JYLU JINAÝ

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Jyly jinaý refers to the collective collection of money, goods or other material assistance for a person or family experiencing hardship.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Жылу жинау
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Jyly jinaý
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ʒɯˈlʊ ʒɯˈnɑw/
     ●​   Word class: Phrase; noun-like expression
     ●​   Related forms: Жылу жинау — to collect assistance; жылу беру — to provide assistance.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Jyly jinaý refers to the collective collection of money, goods or other material assistance for a person or family experiencing
hardship.

The expression combines жылу (jyly, warmth) and жинау (jinaý, to collect). In this context, жылу is metaphorical: it refers to
human support and solidarity rather than physical heat.

The assistance may be organised among relatives, neighbours or a wider community.
sections.Cultural context:
The practice is associated with collective support in Kazakh social life. When a household experienced a serious difficulty, such
as a fire, loss of property or another major misfortune, people could contribute resources to help it recover.

This form of assistance reflects the importance of mutual responsibility and community support. It should not be confused with
asar: asar is primarily associated with collective labour, whereas jyly jinaý concerns the collection of material assistance.
sections.Social function:
●​   Helps households recover from serious hardship.
     ●​   Mobilises resources beyond the affected family's immediate capacity.
     ●​   Strengthens community solidarity.
     ●​   Gives relatives and neighbours a practical way to demonstrate support.
     ●​   Reduces the burden of individual misfortune.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Compassion.
     ●​   Solidarity.
     ●​   Mutual responsibility.
     ●​   Generosity.
     ●​   Collective care.

The practice should not be presented as a formal welfare system. It is a form of community-based assistance, and its
organisation can vary.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Жылу жинау — to organise a collection for someone in need.
     ●​   Жылу жинап беру — to collect and provide assistance.
     ●​   Жылу жинауға қатысу — to participate in a community collection.

Example: After a family's house is damaged by a fire, neighbours and relatives collect money and essential supplies to help
them rebuild their lives.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Community relief collection: Useful when money or goods are collected.
     ●​   Collective material assistance: Describes the mechanism precisely.
     ●​   Community support fund: Suitable only when a formal fund is actually established.
     ●​   Mutual aid: Captures the broader principle but not the specific collection process.
 A literal translation such as collecting warmth would be misleading without cultural explanation.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Jyly jinaý is a practice of collecting material assistance for a person or household facing serious hardship. Relatives,
neighbours and other community members may contribute money, food, clothing or other useful resources.

The word jyly literally relates to warmth, but in this expression it represents human care and support. The idea is that a
community can provide practical help when one household cannot manage a difficult situation alone.

For example, if a family loses its home in a fire, people may organise a collection to help provide shelter, replace essential
belongings or cover immediate expenses. The contributions may be small individually, but together they can make a meaningful
difference.

For an international reader, the most useful explanation is a traditional form of community-based material assistance collected
for people experiencing serious hardship.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: General context of traditional social customs and community relationships.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic source distinguishing jyly jinaý from other forms of mutual aid
           and documenting the circumstances in which it was practised.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; the distinction from asar is a working conceptual distinction that requires source-level
           confirmation.

heading: ENShI

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Enshi refers to property or resources allocated to a married son or a newly established household by the family.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Енші
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Enshi
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /jenˈʃɪ/
     ●​    Word class: Noun
     ●​    Related forms: Енші беру — to provide a share of property; енші бөлу — to divide or allocate a share; еншісін алу
           — to receive one's allocated share.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Enshi refers to property or resources allocated to a married son or a newly established household by the family.

It traditionally could include livestock, household goods or other resources needed to establish an independent household.

The term is connected with the transfer or allocation of family property, rather than an ordinary gift given on a casual occasion.
sections.Cultural context:
The concept is associated with household organisation, inheritance practices and the establishment of new family units in
traditional Kazakh society.

In a pastoral economy, livestock was an important source of wealth and livelihood. Providing a son with an enshi could help him
establish a separate household and begin managing his own economic responsibilities.

The details of allocation could vary across families and historical periods. Enshi should not automatically be equated with
modern legal inheritance, because customary allocation and formal inheritance law are different systems.
sections.Social function:
●​    Supports the establishment of a new household.
     ●​    Transfers resources between generations.
      ●​    Recognises a young family's growing independence.
     ●​    Maintains economic relationships between parents and adult children.
     ●​    Helps distribute family resources.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​    Family responsibility.
     ●​    Intergenerational support.
     ●​    Economic independence.
     ●​    Continuity of the household.
     ●​    Parental care.

The concept should not be interpreted as a universal entitlement with one fixed amount or identical rules in every Kazakh
family.
sections.Practical application:
●​    Енші беру — to allocate property or resources to a newly established household.
     ●​    Енші бөлу — to divide and allocate a household's resources.
     ●​    Енші алған ұл — a son who has received his allocated share.

Example: When a son establishes a separate household, his parents provide him with livestock and household resources to
help him become economically independent.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    Household establishment share: Describes the purpose, though it is not a standard English term.
     ●​    Allocated family property: Emphasises the transfer of resources.
     ●​    Starter provision for a new household: Useful for an international audience.
     ●​    Inheritance: Potentially misleading because enshi may be allocated during the parents' lifetime and serves a specific
           household-establishment function.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Enshi is a customary allocation of family resources that helps a son establish an independent household. In traditional Kazakh
society, this could include livestock, household goods or other property needed to begin a separate family life.

The practice reflects an important transition: a son moves from being part of his parents' household towards managing his own
household, while remaining connected to the wider family. The resources provided are not merely a celebratory present. They
can form part of the material foundation of the new household.

For an international reader, enshi is best explained as a customary share of family property or resources allocated to help
establish a new household. It should be distinguished from inheritance in the strict legal sense and from an ordinary wedding
gift.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: General context of Kazakh family traditions and social organisation.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic or historical source on enshi, including the property allocated,
           recipients and timing.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; the distinction between customary allocation and legal inheritance needs specialist source
           support.

heading: AT MINGIZIP, SHAPAN JABÝ

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: The expression literally means “to provide someone with a horse and place a shapan robe on them.” It describes a traditional form of honouring or rewarding a person through the presentation of significant gifts, especially a horse and a tra

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Ат мінгізіп, шапан жабу
     ●​   Latin transliteration: At mingizip, shapan jabý
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ɑt mɪŋɪˈzɪp ʃɑˈpɑn ʒɑˈbʊ/
     ●​   Word class: Fixed expression; customary phrase
     ●​   Related forms: Ат мінгізу — to present someone with a horse; шапан жабу — to place a traditional robe on someone
          as a gift or sign of honour.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
The expression literally means “to provide someone with a horse and place a shapan robe on them.”

It describes a traditional form of honouring or rewarding a person through the presentation of significant gifts, especially a horse
and a traditional outer garment.

The expression can refer to a gesture of respect, recognition, gratitude or honour.
sections.Cultural context:
The horse had substantial economic, practical and symbolic importance in traditional Kazakh society. A horse could represent
wealth, mobility, livelihood and social standing.

The shapan is a traditional robe or outer garment. Presenting one to someone could serve as a visible expression of respect
and recognition.

Together, a horse and a shapan could form a particularly meaningful gift. The practice is associated with honouring respected
guests, distinguished individuals or people who had performed a significant service.

The exact occasion and meaning depended on historical period, local custom and the relationship between the giver and
recipient.
sections.Social function:
●​   Publicly recognises a person's contribution or status.
     ●​   Expresses respect and gratitude.
     ●​   Strengthens relationships between individuals and families.
     ●​   Creates a visible and memorable gesture of honour.
     ●​   Demonstrates the giver's generosity.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Honour.
     ●​   Respect.
     ●​   Generosity.
     ●​   Recognition.
     ●​   Prestige.
     ●​   Gratitude.

The expression should not be interpreted as a routine gift-giving practice. Its significance lies in the social recognition conveyed
by the gesture.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Ат мінгізіп, шапан жабу — to honour someone by presenting a horse and a traditional robe.
     ●​   Шапан жабу — to honour someone by placing a shapan on their shoulders.
     ●​   Ат мінгізу — to present someone with a horse.

Example: At a public celebration, a respected guest is honoured with a traditional robe and a horse in recognition of their
contribution.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    To honour someone with a horse and a traditional robe: The clearest explanatory translation.
     ●​    Ceremonial presentation of a horse and robe: Useful in formal descriptions.
     ●​    Traditional gift of honour: Concise, but loses the concrete objects.
     ●​    Public gesture of recognition: Captures the social function rather than the literal act.

The phrase should not be translated as simply giving presents, because the particular gifts and their symbolic importance
matter.
sections.Cultural transfer:
At mingizip, shapan jabý describes a traditional gesture of honour in which a person is presented with a horse and a shapan, a
traditional outer robe. Both objects carry cultural significance. The horse was historically important for transport, work, wealth
and social status, while the robe could serve as a visible sign of respect.

The gesture could be used to recognise a distinguished guest, express gratitude or honour someone for a meaningful
contribution. It is not simply about the material value of the gifts. The public act of presenting them communicates that the
recipient is respected.

For an international audience, the expression can be understood as a traditional ceremonial gesture of honour involving the
presentation of a horse and a robe.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: General discussion of traditional customs and material culture.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A historical or ethnographic source documenting the specific ceremonial expression, its
           occasions and its symbolic interpretation.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; the symbolic interpretation of both gifts requires more specific evidence.

heading: BATA

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Bata refers to a spoken blessing, usually expressed as a wish for well-being, prosperity, protection or success.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Бата
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Bata
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /bɑˈtɑ/
     ●​    Word class: Noun
     ●​    Related forms: Бата беру — to give a blessing; бата алу — to receive a blessing; баталы сөз — words of blessing.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Bata refers to a spoken blessing, usually expressed as a wish for well-being, prosperity, protection or success.

It is commonly delivered by an elder or another respected person, although the speaker and occasion may vary.

A bata can be short or elaborate and may include wishes for health, a safe journey, family prosperity, good fortune or success in
an important undertaking.
sections.Cultural context:
Bata is an important practice in Kazakh oral tradition. It is associated with family occasions, meals, celebrations, journeys and
significant life events.

Research on bata beru documents both traditional forms and changes in contemporary practice. It also shows that the practice
should be understood as a living tradition rather than something frozen in the past.

A bata may contain religious language, references to God or expressions of moral wisdom. However, not every bata should be
treated as identical to a formal religious prayer.
sections.Social function:
●​    Expresses goodwill and support.
     ●​    Recognises the speaker's relationship with the recipient.
     ●​    Marks important moments and transitions.
     ●​    Transmits moral expectations and cultural language.
     ●​    Strengthens intergenerational relationships.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​    Blessing and goodwill.
     ●​    Respect for elders.
     ●​    Spiritual guidance.
     ●​    Hope and protection.
     ●​    Intergenerational continuity.

The concept should not be reduced to a magical formula. Its meaning lies in spoken goodwill, cultural practice and the
relationship between the people involved.
sections.Practical application:
●​    Бата беру — to give a blessing.
     ●​    Бата алу — to receive a blessing.
     ●​    Ақ бата — a positive or heartfelt blessing.
     ●​    Батаңды бер — give your blessing.

Example: Before a young person begins a journey, an elder gives a bata, wishing them safety, success and a good return.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    Blessing: The closest general equivalent.
     ●​    Spoken blessing: Emphasises that it is delivered orally.
     ●​    Benediction: Appropriate in formal or religious contexts, but may sound too specifically Christian in English.
     ●​    Prayer: Suitable for some examples, but not all bata are formal prayers.
     ●​    Words of goodwill: Useful when the content is primarily a wish for someone's success.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Bata is a spoken blessing given to express goodwill and wish someone well. It may be offered before a journey, at the end of a
meal, during a family celebration or at another important moment. The speaker often wishes the recipient health, prosperity,
protection, success and a good future.

The person giving a bata may be an elder or someone respected by the family or community. In many settings, the act of
receiving a blessing is also a way of showing respect and recognising the speaker's experience.

A bata can contain religious references, but it is not always identical to a formal prayer. It may also include poetic expressions,
moral advice and traditional wishes.

For an international reader, bata is best understood as a traditional spoken blessing that expresses goodwill, moral support and
wishes for well-being.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Sarsambekova et al. (2021). “Bata Beru in Kazakh Culture – Traditions and Innovations.” Vestnik NSU. Series:
           History and Philology, 20(3), 131–141. DOI: 10.25205/1818-7919-2021-20-3-131-141. Article PDF
     ●​    Supports: The practice of giving bata, its cultural role, traditional forms and contemporary changes.
     ●​    Page range: 131–141 for the article as a whole. Individual claims should be matched to the relevant page before final
           publication.
     ●​    Verification status: Dedicated academic research identified; detailed page-level claim verification remains necessary.

heading: TILEK

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Tilek means a wish, hope or expression of goodwill directed towards another person.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Тілек
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Tilek
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /tɪˈlek/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Тілек айту — to express a wish; тілек білдіру — to convey one's wishes; ақ тілек — a sincere or
          good wish.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Tilek means a wish, hope or expression of goodwill directed towards another person.

It can refer to an ordinary personal wish, a congratulatory message or a more formal expression of good intentions on an
important occasion.

Unlike bata, which is often associated with a spoken blessing and a recognised cultural practice, tilek has a broader everyday
meaning.
sections.Cultural context:
Expressing good wishes is an important part of social interaction in Kazakh-speaking communities. People offer tilek during
birthdays, weddings, holidays, achievements and other significant events.

The expression may be personal and informal or delivered in front of a group during a celebration.

It can overlap with bata, but the two terms should not be treated as interchangeable. A tilek is generally a wish, while a bata is a
culturally recognised form of blessing.
sections.Social function:
●​   Communicates goodwill and emotional support.
     ●​   Recognises another person's achievement or important occasion.
     ●​   Maintains friendly and family relationships.
     ●​   Creates a positive atmosphere during social gatherings.
     ●​   Allows people to express hopes for one another.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Goodwill.
     ●​   Kindness.
     ●​   Optimism.
     ●​   Care.
     ●​   Social connection.

A tilek does not necessarily carry religious or ceremonial significance. Its meaning depends on the context and wording.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Тілек айту — to express a wish.
     ●​   Туған күнге тілек айту — to give birthday wishes.
     ●​   Ақ тілегін білдіру — to express sincere good wishes.
     ●​   Тілегің қабыл болсын — may your wish be fulfilled.

Example: At a friend's graduation, someone expresses a tilek wishing them success in their future studies and career.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Wish: The most direct and flexible equivalent.
     ●​   Good wishes: Suitable for congratulations and social occasions.
      ●​    Expression of goodwill: Emphasises the social function.
     ●​    Hope: Appropriate when referring to a desired future outcome.
     ●​    Blessing: Possible in certain contexts, but may incorrectly suggest the more specific practice of bata.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Tilek is an expression of a person's wishes or hopes for someone else. It can be used in everyday conversation, at family
celebrations, during public events or when congratulating someone on an achievement.

For example, at a wedding, a person may express wishes for the couple's happiness and a successful family life. At a
graduation, someone may wish the graduate success in their future career.

The important distinction is that tilek is a broad concept. It does not always involve a formal speaker, a particular ritual or
religious language. A bata, by contrast, is a more specific culturally recognised form of spoken blessing.

For an international reader, tilek can be explained as a spoken or written expression of good wishes, hope and goodwill towards
another person.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Sarsambekova et al. (2021). “Bata Beru in Kazakh Culture – Traditions and Innovations.” Vestnik NSU. Series:
           History and Philology, 20(3), 131–141. Article PDF
     ●​    Supports: The cultural context of spoken blessings and their relationship to social occasions.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated linguistic source on tilek, especially its semantic range and distinction from
           bata.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; the distinction is a working linguistic explanation requiring dedicated source confirmation.

heading: AGAYYNGERShILIK

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Aǵayynǵershilik refers to the conduct, solidarity and mutual responsibility expected or demonstrated among relatives and people connected through kinship.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Ағайынгершілік
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Aǵayynǵershilik
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /ɑʁɑjɯŋʁeɾˈʃɪlɪk/
     ●​    Word class: Noun
     ●​    Related forms: Ағайын — relatives or kin; ағайынгершілік таныту — to demonstrate kin solidarity; ағайындық —
           kinship or relatedness.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Aǵayynǵershilik refers to the conduct, solidarity and mutual responsibility expected or demonstrated among relatives and
people connected through kinship.

It describes more than the fact of being related. It concerns how people behave towards one another because of their family or
kin relationships.

Depending on context, it may refer to support, cooperation, reconciliation or the fulfilment of responsibilities among relatives.
sections.Cultural context:
Kinship has historically played an important role in Kazakh social organisation. Relationships between relatives could influence
mutual assistance, household cooperation, marriage connections and participation in family events.

Aǵayynǵershilik expresses the expectation that kinship should be reflected in conduct: relatives should not remain indifferent
when another family member needs help.

However, it should not be interpreted as meaning that every relative has the same obligations or that all family relationships are
harmonious. Actual responsibilities vary according to closeness, circumstances and social expectations.
sections.Social function:
●​    Encourages assistance among relatives.
     ●​    Maintains relationships across extended families.
     ●​    Supports cooperation during important events and difficult situations.
     ●​    Creates expectations of responsibility and reciprocity.
     ●​    Helps preserve family and kinship networks.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​    Family solidarity.
     ●​    Mutual responsibility.
     ●​    Loyalty.
     ●​    Cooperation.
     ●​    Reconciliation.
     ●​    Care for relatives.

A critical explanation should also recognise that kinship obligations can create pressure or conflict. Solidarity is a social
expectation, not proof that every relationship is positive.
sections.Practical application:
●​    Ағайынгершілік таныту — to show solidarity with relatives.
     ●​    Ағайынгершілік жасау — to act in accordance with kinship responsibilities.
     ●​    Ағайынгершілікпен көмектесу — to help someone out of kinship solidarity.

Example: When a relative experiences financial or personal hardship, other family members organise support and help them
manage the situation.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    Kin solidarity: The most concise conceptual equivalent.
     ●​    Family solidarity: More accessible to general readers, although it may imply only the immediate family.
     ●​    Mutual responsibility among relatives: The most precise explanatory translation.
     ●​    Kinship-based support: Emphasises assistance rooted in family relationships.
     ●​    Family loyalty: Captures one aspect but does not fully express practical cooperation.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Aǵayynǵershilik describes the idea that relationships between relatives should involve practical care, support and responsibility.
It is not merely a label for biological or genealogical connection. It concerns the way people act because they belong to an
extended family network.

For example, when a relative faces a difficult situation, other family members may contribute money, offer accommodation, help
with work or take part in resolving the problem. Such assistance can be understood as an expression of aǵayynǵershilik.

The concept is connected to the wider importance of kinship in Kazakh social life. However, it should not be presented as an
ideal that every family always fulfils. Relationships can involve disagreement, unequal expectations and conflict.

For an international reader, aǵayynǵershilik is best explained as a principle of kinship-based solidarity and mutual responsibility
among relatives.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: General context of traditional social relationships and family customs.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated linguistic or ethnographic source on the term aǵayynǵershilik itself.
           Research on aǵayyn or kinship in general cannot automatically establish every nuance of this derived term.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; the social interpretation needs a dedicated source.

heading: JOMARTTYQ

category.title: Hospitality and Mutual Assistance
category.description: Practices of welcome, reciprocity and community support.

short: Jomarttyq refers to generosity: the willingness to share one's resources, offer assistance and give to others without focusing exclusively on personal benefit.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Жомарттық
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Jomarttyq
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ʒɔmɑɾtˈtɯq/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Жомарт — generous; жомарт адам — a generous person; жомарттық таныту — to demonstrate
          generosity.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Jomarttyq refers to generosity: the willingness to share one's resources, offer assistance and give to others without focusing
exclusively on personal benefit.

It can describe generosity with money, food, possessions, time or effort.

The word may refer to a personal quality as well as conduct demonstrated through particular actions.
sections.Cultural context:
Generosity is an important moral value in many societies, including Kazakh cultural traditions. It can be expressed through
hospitality, assistance to relatives and neighbours, support for people experiencing hardship and giving to guests.

In Kazakh social life, generosity may be connected with the expectation that people should share what they have and avoid
excessive selfishness.

However, jomarttyq should not be treated as identical to every form of hospitality or mutual aid. It is a broader personal and
moral quality that can be expressed through different practices.
sections.Social function:
●​   Encourages people to share resources.
     ●​   Supports individuals and households in need.
     ●​   Strengthens relationships through giving.
     ●​   Reinforces positive social reputation.
     ●​   Contributes to reciprocal and cooperative relationships.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Generosity.
     ●​   Kindness.
     ●​   Selflessness.
     ●​   Open-handedness.
     ●​   Compassion.
     ●​   Social responsibility.

Generosity should not be confused with unlimited giving. A person can be generous while still maintaining reasonable personal
and family boundaries.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Жомарт адам — a generous person.
     ●​   Жомарттық таныту — to show generosity.
     ●​   Жомарттық жасау — to act generously.
     ●​   Жомарт мінез — a generous disposition.

Example: A person regularly shares food with neighbours, supports people in need and offers help without expecting an
immediate reward.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    Generosity: The best general equivalent.
     ●​    Benevolence: Emphasises goodwill and concern for others, often in a more formal register.
     ●​    Open-handedness: Highlights willingness to give material resources.
     ●​    Liberality: Can describe generosity, but may sound formal or archaic.
     ●​    Selflessness: Captures willingness to put others first, but is not identical to generosity.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Jomarttyq is the quality of being generous and willing to share with others. It may be expressed through giving food to guests,
supporting relatives, helping neighbours or contributing resources to people experiencing hardship.

The concept concerns both attitude and action. A generous person is not simply someone who gives expensive gifts.
Generosity can also be demonstrated through time, effort, attention and practical assistance.

In Kazakh social contexts, jomarttyq may be associated with hospitality and mutual support, but it is broader than either
practice. Hospitality concerns the reception of guests, while asar and jyly jinaý describe particular forms of collective
assistance. Jomarttyq describes the generous disposition that can motivate many different actions.

For an international reader, jomarttyq can be understood as a moral quality of generosity expressed through sharing, giving and
helping others.
sections.Evidence:
●​    Smagulova, G. N., & Makataeva, Sh. M. (2020). “Лингвоаксиология: қазақтар дүниетанымындағы құндылықтар
           ұғымы.” Eurasian Journal of Philology: Science and Education, 177(1), 187–193. DOI:
           10.26577/EJPh.2020.v177.i1.ph26. Article
     ●​    Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
           Society.” PDF
     ●​    Supports: Broader discussion of cultural values and traditional social practices.
     ●​    Additional evidence needed: A dedicated linguistic study of jomarttyq and its relationship to generosity, hospitality and
           giving.
     ●​    Verification status: Draft; relevant broader research identified, but direct evidence for the term's full semantic range
           remains necessary.

III. Family, Kinship and Generational
Continuity — 36–50
This category is particularly important because Kazakh kinship vocabulary is highly specific. English often uses one broad word
such as relative, in-law or ancestor where Kazakh distinguishes several relationships.

The entries below preserve those distinctions. In particular, naǵashy, zhiyen, böle, quda, qudaǵy and abysyn are not
interchangeable family labels. Their meaning depends on exactly how two people are related.

Transliteration note: I use a consistent working Latin form throughout this category. These spellings are for the project and
should not be presented as the only officially established Latin orthography.

heading: JETI ATA

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Jeti ata literally means “seven ancestors” or “seven generations of ancestors.” It refers to the traditional practice of tracing one's paternal lineage across seven generations.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Жеті ата
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Jeti ata
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /ʒeˈtɪ ɑˈtɑ/
     ●​    Word class: Noun phrase
     ●​    Related forms: Жеті атасын білу — to know one's seven ancestors; жеті атаға толмай — before seven ancestral
           generations have passed; шежіре — genealogy or genealogical record.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Jeti ata literally means “seven ancestors” or “seven generations of ancestors.” It refers to the traditional practice of tracing one's
paternal lineage across seven generations.

The expression is closely connected with genealogical knowledge, family identity and customary marriage restrictions. In
traditional explanations, people belonging to the same paternal lineage were expected to know their common ancestry and
avoid marriage within the prohibited degree of kinship.

The precise way generations are counted and named should be established from the relevant genealogical tradition rather than
assumed to be identical in every region or family.
sections.Cultural context:
Knowledge of jeti ata has been an important element of traditional Kazakh kinship organisation. Genealogical knowledge was
transmitted orally through family histories and shezhire.

The practice helped people identify their paternal relatives, understand their place within a wider lineage and observe
customary marriage restrictions. It also preserved historical memory by connecting living generations with their ancestors.

It should not be described as a simple biological rule applying identically to every Kazakh community throughout history.
Customary practice, genealogical accounts and modern legal marriage regulations are different matters.
sections.Social function:
●​   Preserves knowledge of paternal ancestry.
     ●​   Helps identify kinship relationships.
     ●​   Supports customary marriage restrictions.
     ●​   Connects individuals to extended family networks.
     ●​   Transmits family history between generations.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Respect for ancestors.
     ●​   Family continuity.
     ●​   Genealogical memory.
     ●​   Responsibility towards relatives.
     ●​   Awareness of one's origins.

The concept should not be reduced to memorising seven names. Its significance lies in the relationship between genealogy,
social identity and customary rules.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Жеті атасын білу — to know one's seven generations of paternal ancestors.
     ●​   Жеті атаға толмай қыз алыспау — the customary prohibition against marrying within the restricted paternal lineage
          before the required generations have passed.
     ●​   Жеті атасын тарату — to trace or recite one's paternal genealogy.

Example: A young person asks an older relative to explain the family's paternal genealogy and learns the names and
relationships of ancestors across seven generations.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Seven-generation paternal genealogy: The most precise explanatory translation.
     ●​   Seven ancestors: A literal translation, but it may not communicate the wider social meaning.
      ●​   Seven-generation lineage rule: Useful when discussing marriage customs.
     ●​   Ancestral lineage tradition: Captures the broader cultural significance but loses the number seven.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Jeti ata is a Kazakh tradition of knowing and tracing one's paternal ancestry across seven generations. It connects a person to
a wider network of relatives and ancestors, rather than defining family only through parents and grandparents.

This knowledge has practical social significance. It can help people identify whether they share a paternal lineage and
understand customary restrictions on marriage within that lineage. Genealogical knowledge is also a way of preserving family
history: older generations transmit names, relationships and stories to younger members.

For someone unfamiliar with Kazakhstan, it is important to understand that jeti ata is not simply a list of seven relatives. It is a
system of genealogical awareness connected to identity, social relationships and customary marriage rules. Its specific
application should be explained with attention to historical and regional variation.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Supports: Broader research context on Kazakh cultural concepts and traditional social organisation.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic or historical study of jeti ata, including the exact
          generation-counting system and marriage restrictions.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the central description is established in general accounts of Kazakh kinship, but exact
          genealogical details and page references require verification.

heading: RU

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Ru refers to a clan or lineage group whose members recognise a shared ancestry.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Ру
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Ru
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ɾʊ/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Рулық — clan-related; рулас — belonging to the same clan or lineage group; руын білу — to know
          one's clan affiliation.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Ru refers to a clan or lineage group whose members recognise a shared ancestry.

In Kazakh social and historical contexts, the term is used to identify a person's affiliation with a particular kinship group. It may
be associated with genealogical descent, collective identity and relationships between extended families.

A ru is not necessarily equivalent to a small nuclear family or a modern administrative community.
sections.Cultural context:
Clans and lineage groups formed part of the traditional organisation of Kazakh society. Genealogical connections could
influence social relationships, marriage considerations, mutual assistance and collective identity.

Knowledge of one's ru was often connected to knowledge of shezhire, or genealogy. However, a person's clan affiliation should
not be treated as a complete description of their identity or as evidence that all members of a clan have identical interests.

The term also needs historical care: clan structures and their political or social importance changed over time.
sections.Social function:
●​   Identifies a person's lineage affiliation.
     ●​   Organises genealogical knowledge.
     ●​   Helps establish certain kinship relationships.
     ●​   Can influence customary marriage considerations.
     ●​   Provides a framework for collective identity and historical memory.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Ancestral continuity.
     ●​   Belonging.
     ●​   Family history.
     ●​   Collective memory.
     ●​   Kinship solidarity.

The concept should not be romanticised or treated as a fixed political identity. It should also not be confused with ethnicity,
citizenship or a modern political organisation.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Қай рудансың? — Which clan or lineage group do you belong to?
     ●​   Рулас адамдар — people belonging to the same clan.
     ●​   Руын білу — to know one's clan affiliation.

Example: During a family conversation, an older relative explains which ru the family belongs to and how it connects to a wider
genealogical network.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Clan: The most practical general equivalent.
     ●​   Lineage group: Useful when emphasising descent and genealogy.
     ●​   Kinship group: Broader and less specific.
     ●​   Tribal group: May be appropriate in some historical contexts, but can exaggerate or distort the structure.

Clan is generally suitable, but the entry should retain the Kazakh term because the historical organisation of ru does not always
correspond exactly to English-language anthropological categories.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Ru is a traditional Kazakh clan or lineage group associated with shared ancestry. It connects individuals and families to a wider
genealogical structure. A person may know their ru as part of understanding their family history and their relationship to other
people.

Historically, such affiliations could influence marriage customs, mutual assistance and social organisation. However, clan
affiliation is only one dimension of identity. It does not determine a person's personality, political views, social status or
individual choices.

For an international reader, ru can be understood as a traditional kinship-based clan or lineage group recognised through
shared ancestry. The term should be explained historically and socially rather than treated as a direct equivalent of a modern
tribe or ethnic group.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
      ●​   Supports: General cultural and social context of traditional kinship structures.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A specialist historical or anthropological source on the structure and historical
          development of Kazakh ru groups.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the general meaning is clear, but historical classifications and regional differences need
          specialist verification.

heading: JUZ

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Juz refers to one of the three major historical groupings traditionally used to describe the organisation of Kazakh society: ●​ Ұлы жүз — Senior Jüz.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Жүз
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Juz
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ʒʏz/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Ұлы жүз — Senior Jüz; Орта жүз — Middle Jüz; Кіші жүз — Junior Jüz; жүздік құрылым — a
          Jüz-based structure.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Juz refers to one of the three major historical groupings traditionally used to describe the organisation of Kazakh society:

     ●​   Ұлы жүз — Senior Jüz.
     ●​   Орта жүз — Middle Jüz.
     ●​   Кіші жүз — Junior Jüz.

The term can also mean “hundred” in other linguistic contexts, but in Kazakh historical and cultural discussion it commonly
refers to these three large groupings.
sections.Cultural context:
The three Jüz groupings are an important feature of traditional Kazakh historical and social organisation. They were associated
with broad territorial, genealogical and political networks.

Their historical formation and exact origins are subjects of scholarly discussion. It would be inaccurate to present one simple
explanation as universally accepted.

The Jüz system should not be described as three separate ethnic groups. The three groupings existed within the wider Kazakh
people and were connected through shared language, culture and historical identity.

Nor should historical Jüz affiliation be assumed to determine how every Kazakh person identifies today.
sections.Social function:
●​   Organised broad genealogical and social affiliations.
     ●​   Provided a framework for historical political and territorial relationships.
     ●​   Helped structure some forms of collective identity.
     ●​   Appears in historical accounts of leadership, alliances and social organisation.
     ●​   Preserves an important element of Kazakh historical memory.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Historical identity.
     ●​   Collective memory.
     ●​   Ancestral affiliation.
     ●​   Regional and genealogical belonging.
     ●​   Continuity of the Kazakh people.
 The concept must be handled carefully: it should not be used to claim that one Jüz is superior to another or to assign fixed
characteristics to their members.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Ұлы жүзденмін — I belong to the Senior Jüz.
     ●​   Орта жүз — the Middle Jüz.
     ●​   Кіші жүз — the Junior Jüz.
     ●​   Қазақтың үш жүзі — the three Jüz groupings of the Kazakh people.

Example: A historian explains the three Jüz groupings when describing the political and social organisation of the Kazakh
steppe in a particular historical period.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Jüz: Best retained as a transliterated cultural term.
     ●​   Historical confederation: May be useful in some historical explanations, but can imply a specific political structure that
          requires evidence.
     ●​   Genealogical grouping: Emphasises kinship and descent.
     ●​   Historical social grouping: A broad and cautious explanatory equivalent.

Avoid translating Jüz simply as tribe. It refers to a larger and historically more complex grouping.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Juz refers to one of three major historical groupings of the Kazakh people: the Senior, Middle and Junior Jüz. These groupings
played a role in the traditional organisation of Kazakh society and were connected with broad genealogical, territorial and
political relationships.

They should not be understood as three separate nationalities or ethnic groups. Rather, they were historical structures within
the wider Kazakh community. Their origins, development and political significance have been interpreted differently by
historians.

For an international reader, the safest explanation is one of the three major historical social and genealogical groupings of the
Kazakh people. The original term should be retained because no single English word captures its full historical meaning.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: General context of traditional Kazakh social organisation and cultural concepts.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: Specialist historical scholarship on the origins, chronology, territorial organisation and
          political role of the three Jüz groupings.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; historical interpretation requires more specialised sources than a general traditions study.

heading: ATA JURT

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Ata jurt refers to the ancestral homeland or the land associated with one's forebears.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Ата жұрт
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Ata jurt
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ɑˈtɑ ʒʊɾt/
     ●​   Word class: Noun phrase
     ●​   Related forms: Ата-баба — ancestors; жұрт — people, homeland or settlement, depending on context; ата қоныс —
          ancestral settlement or homeland.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Ata jurt refers to the ancestral homeland or the land associated with one's forebears.

The expression combines ata (ancestor or forefather) and jurt (homeland, settlement or community). It can refer to a place
connected with family origins and inherited historical memory.

Its meaning may overlap with ata qonys, but the two expressions should not automatically be treated as identical in every
context.
sections.Cultural context:
The idea of ancestral land has significance in Kazakh historical memory and cultural identity. For communities whose
livelihoods were connected to movement across the steppe, land could be associated with seasonal routes, settlement areas,
family histories and collective belonging.

Ata jurt may also be used in broader discussions of homeland and national identity. Its meaning therefore depends on whether
the speaker is discussing family ancestry, a historical homeland or a wider national idea.

It should not automatically be translated as the modern nation-state or equated with a precise legal territory.
sections.Social function:
●​   Connects individuals with ancestral places.
     ●​   Preserves family and community memory.
     ●​   Expresses belonging to a historical homeland.
     ●​   Provides language for discussing displacement, return and continuity.
     ●​   Links personal identity with collective history.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Ancestral belonging.
     ●​   Historical memory.
     ●​   Continuity.
     ●​   Attachment to land.
     ●​   Cultural identity.

The concept should not be interpreted as a claim that every person has one fixed ancestral location or that all historical
territorial boundaries were identical to modern borders.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Ата жұртқа оралу — to return to the ancestral homeland.
     ●​   Ата жұртты аңсау — to long for one's ancestral homeland.
     ●​   Ата жұрт тарихы — the history of the ancestral homeland.

Example: A family tells younger generations about the region from which their ancestors came and why it remains important to
their family identity.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Ancestral homeland: The most suitable general equivalent.
     ●​   Land of one's ancestors: Clear and accessible.
     ●​   Ancestral land: Useful when the emphasis is on territory and land.
     ●​   Homeland: Too broad on its own because it does not necessarily express the ancestral dimension.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Ata jurt refers to a homeland or place connected with one's ancestors. It expresses a relationship between people, land and
historical memory. The place may be remembered through family stories, historical records or the wider traditions of a
community.

The expression can be used in a personal sense, when someone speaks about the homeland of their ancestors, or in a broader
cultural sense, when discussing the historical homeland of a people.

For an international audience, ata jurt is best explained as the ancestral homeland: a place associated with one's forebears and
inherited sense of belonging. It is important to distinguish this idea from citizenship or the legal territory of a modern state.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Supports: Broader context of national concepts, cultural identity and traditional social life.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated linguistic or historical study distinguishing ata jurt, ata qonys, tugan jer and
          Otan.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; semantic distinctions require more direct evidence.

heading: TÝǴAN JER

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Tuǵan jer literally means “the land where one was born.” It refers to a person's birthplace or native place and may also express emotional attachment to the wider region in which they grew up.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Туған жер
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Tuǵan jer
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /tʊˈʁɑn ʒeɾ/
     ●​   Word class: Noun phrase
     ●​   Related forms: Туған ел — one's native country or people; туған өлке — one's native region; туған жерге оралу —
          to return to one's birthplace or homeland.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Tuǵan jer literally means “the land where one was born.”

It refers to a person's birthplace or native place and may also express emotional attachment to the wider region in which they
grew up.

Depending on context, the phrase can describe a specific village, town, city, region or a more broadly imagined homeland.
sections.Cultural context:
Attachment to one's birthplace and native land appears in Kazakh literature, oral tradition and public discourse. The concept
can connect personal memories with family history, landscape and a sense of belonging.

For people whose families have moved between regions or countries, tuǵan jer may refer to the place of birth, the place of
upbringing or the place regarded as home through family connection.

It should be distinguished from Otan, which generally carries a broader meaning of homeland or country, and from ata jurt,
which emphasises ancestral homeland.
sections.Social function:
●​   Expresses attachment to one's birthplace.
     ●​   Connects personal identity with a particular place.
      ●​   Preserves memories of childhood and family.
     ●​   Provides language for discussing return and belonging.
     ●​   Can encourage responsibility towards one's native region.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Belonging.
     ●​   Memory.
     ●​   Attachment to land.
     ●​   Family roots.
     ●​   Responsibility towards one's community.

The concept should not be reduced to nationalism. A person may feel attachment to a birthplace without identifying it as their
only homeland or permanent place of residence.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Туған жерді сағыну — to miss one's native place.
     ●​   Туған жерге оралу — to return to one's birthplace or native region.
     ●​   Туған жердің табиғаты — the natural environment of one's native land.
     ●​   Туған жерге қызмет ету — to serve or contribute to one's native region.

Example: A person who has moved abroad speaks about returning to the village where they grew up and visiting their family.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Birthplace: Accurate when referring to the exact place of birth.
     ●​   Native place: Useful when referring to a town, village or region.
     ●​   Homeland: Appropriate in some emotional or broader contexts, but can be too expansive.
     ●​   Native land: Captures emotional attachment to a place.
     ●​   Place of origin: More neutral and formal.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Tuǵan jer is the place where a person was born or grew up, and it often carries emotional significance beyond its geographical
meaning. It can refer to a village, town, city or region associated with childhood, family and personal memories.

Someone living far away may still describe their birthplace as tuǵan jer, expressing a lasting connection to the place even after
moving elsewhere.

The concept is related to homeland, but it is not identical to the idea of a nation-state. It often begins with a personal
relationship to a particular place and can expand into a wider sense of belonging.

For an international reader, tuǵan jer can be understood as one's native place or birthplace, often carrying a strong emotional
connection to family, memory and local identity.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Smagulova, G. N., & Makataeva, Sh. M. (2020). “Лингвоаксиология: қазақтар дүниетанымындағы құндылықтар
          ұғымы.” Eurasian Journal of Philology: Science and Education, 177(1), 187–193. Article
     ●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: Broader discussion of cultural values and national concepts.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated linguistic study comparing tuǵan jer, ata jurt, tuǵan el and Otan.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; general meaning is clear, but its cultural and semantic distinctions need direct textual
          evidence.

heading: NAǴASHY

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Naǵashy refers to relatives on the mother's side of the family.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Нағашы
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Naǵashy
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /nɑˈʁɑʃɯ/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Нағашы жұрт — the mother's side of the family; нағашы ата — maternal grandfather; нағашы әже —
