          maternal grandmother; нағашы аға — maternal uncle or mother's brother, depending on context.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Naǵashy refers to relatives on the mother's side of the family.

It is a kinship term that identifies the maternal side of a person's extended family. Depending on the context, it may refer to a
particular maternal relative or to maternal relatives collectively.

The phrase naǵashy jurt refers more broadly to the mother's family and kinship network.
sections.Cultural context:
Kazakh kinship vocabulary distinguishes maternal and paternal relationships in ways that are not always captured by the
general English word relatives.

The maternal side can have a recognised place in family relationships and customary interaction. The term is therefore
important for understanding how people identify relatives and describe their family networks.

However, the exact meaning of naǵashy in a sentence depends on the person being discussed. It should not automatically be
translated as uncle or grandfather without identifying the relationship.
sections.Social function:
●​   Identifies the maternal side of the family.
     ●​   Helps distinguish maternal and paternal relatives.
     ●​   Supports the organisation of family relationships.
     ●​   Provides specific terms for addressing and referring to relatives.
     ●​   Preserves distinctions within extended kinship networks.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Maternal family connection.
     ●​   Extended kinship.
     ●​   Family continuity.
     ●​   Respect for relatives.
     ●​   Intergenerational relationships.

The term should not be used to imply that maternal relatives have identical roles in every family.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Нағашы жұрт — the mother's side of the family.
     ●​   Нағашы атам — my maternal grandfather.
     ●​   Нағашы ағам — my maternal uncle.
     ●​   Нағашыларыма бардым — I visited my maternal relatives.
 Example: A person says they are visiting their naǵashy jurt during a holiday, meaning they are visiting relatives on their
mother's side.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Maternal relatives: The most accurate general equivalent.
     ●​   Mother's side of the family: The clearest explanatory translation.
     ●​   Maternal kin: More academic or anthropological.
     ●​   Maternal uncle: Correct only when the context identifies a particular uncle.
     ●​   Maternal grandfather: Correct only when referring to the mother's father.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Naǵashy is a Kazakh kinship term for relatives on the mother's side of the family. English often uses the general word relatives
or requires a longer expression such as my mother's family. Kazakh has a specific term that identifies this side of the family
directly.

For example, when someone says they are visiting their naǵashy jurt, they mean that they are visiting their maternal relatives.
The phrase does not identify one particular person; it refers to a wider family network.

This distinction matters because Kazakh kinship terminology can specify relationships that English expresses only through
longer descriptions. For an international reader, naǵashy is best understood as a relative or group of relatives belonging to
one's maternal family.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: Broader linguistic and cultural context of Kazakh kinship concepts.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated Kazakh kinship terminology study documenting the precise range of
          naǵashy and its related forms.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the basic kinship distinction is clear, but the lexical range requires specialist verification.

heading: JHIYEN

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Zhiyen traditionally refers to the child of a person's sister, that is, a nephew or niece on the sister's side.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Жиен
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Zhiyen
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ʒɪˈjen/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Жиен қыз — a sister's daughter; жиен ұл — a sister's son; жиендік — a relationship or customary
          association connected with being a zhiyen.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Zhiyen traditionally refers to the child of a person's sister, that is, a nephew or niece on the sister's side.

The term is more specific than the English words nephew and niece, which do not distinguish whether the child is related
through a brother or a sister.

In traditional kinship descriptions, the relationship between a person and their zhiyen may carry particular customary
expectations and forms of interaction.
sections.Cultural context:
The term is part of the detailed structure of Kazakh kinship vocabulary. It identifies a specific relationship within the extended
family and helps distinguish relatives according to the line through which they are connected.
 Traditional accounts also describe special customs associated with the zhiyen relationship. These should be investigated
individually rather than assumed to apply uniformly to all families or regions.

It is especially important not to confuse zhiyen with böle: the terms identify different kinship connections.
sections.Social function:
●​   Identifies a specific relationship between an individual and their sister's children.
     ●​   Distinguishes this relationship from other types of nephew or niece.
     ●​   Helps organise extended family interactions.
     ●​   Preserves precise genealogical relationships.
     ●​   Supports the transmission of kinship terminology.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Extended family connection.
     ●​   Maternal and paternal kinship distinctions.
     ●​   Family continuity.
     ●​   Recognition of particular relationships.

The term should not be interpreted as a general label for every nephew or niece.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Жиенім — my sister's child.
     ●​   Жиен ұл — sister's son.
     ●​   Жиен қыз — sister's daughter.
     ●​   Жиен нағашыларына барды — the zhiyen visited their maternal relatives.

Example: A woman introduces her sister's son as her zhiyen, using a specific kinship term rather than the broader English word
nephew.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Sister's child: The most precise gender-neutral explanation.
     ●​   Sister's son: Accurate for a male child.
     ●​   Sister's daughter: Accurate for a female child.
     ●​   Nephew / niece: Useful in general English, but loses the exact kinship distinction.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Zhiyen is a Kazakh kinship term traditionally used for the child of one's sister. In English, the words nephew and niece describe
a sibling's child but do not indicate whether the child belongs to the brother's or sister's side.

Kazakh terminology preserves this distinction. The term therefore communicates more information about the family relationship
than its closest everyday English equivalents.

For an international reader, zhiyen is best explained as one's sister's child, either a son or a daughter. It is important to retain
the Kazakh word in the card because a single English equivalent cannot express the full genealogical detail.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: Broader study of Kazakh national and linguistic concepts.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A specialist dictionary or anthropological study confirming the exact kinship definition
          and historical customs associated with zhiyen.
      ●​   Verification status: Draft; the definition should be checked against an authoritative Kazakh kinship dictionary before
          publication.

heading: BÖLE

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Böle refers to children of sisters: two people whose mothers are sisters are böle to one another.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Бөле
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Böle
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /bøˈle/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Бөлелер — cousins of this relationship; бөле болу — to be related as böle.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Böle refers to children of sisters: two people whose mothers are sisters are böle to one another.

The term identifies a specific cousin relationship. English generally translates it as cousin, but that word does not preserve the
fact that the mothers are sisters.
sections.Cultural context:
The term belongs to the detailed system of Kazakh kinship vocabulary. It allows speakers to identify a family relationship more
precisely than English does.

It is particularly useful for describing connections between maternal relatives and distinguishing them from other cousin
relationships.

The term should not be confused with zhiyen. A zhiyen is traditionally the child of one's sister; böle describes the relationship
between children of sisters.
sections.Social function:
●​   Identifies a specific cousin relationship.
     ●​   Preserves distinctions within extended family networks.
     ●​   Helps people describe maternal family connections.
     ●​   Supports accurate genealogical understanding.
     ●​   Maintains culturally specific kinship vocabulary.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Extended family connection.
     ●​   Maternal kinship.
     ●​   Family continuity.
     ●​   Recognition of relationships between households.

The term itself describes a relationship; it does not automatically imply a particular level of closeness or obligation.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Олар бөле — they are cousins whose mothers are sisters.
     ●​   Бөлем — my cousin of this specific relationship.
     ●​   Бөлелер кездесті — the cousins met.
 Example: Two people discover that their mothers are sisters and explain that they are böle.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Cousin: The simplest general equivalent.
     ●​   Maternal cousin: Useful in a broad explanation, though it may not fully specify the relationship.
     ●​   Child of one's mother's sister: The most precise genealogical explanation.
     ●​   Cross-cousin: An anthropological term that may be relevant in technical analysis, but should not be used without
          explaining the exact relationship.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Böle describes the relationship between two people whose mothers are sisters. In English, both people would normally be
called cousins. Kazakh uses a more specific term that identifies the exact family connection.

For example, if two women are sisters, their children are böle to each other. This distinction helps speakers describe extended
family relationships without needing a long explanation.

The term should not be confused with every kind of cousin. It refers to one particular relationship within the wider kinship
system.

For an international reader, böle is best explained as a cousin whose mother is one's mother's sister.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: General linguistic and cultural context of Kazakh kinship concepts.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A specialist kinship dictionary or anthropological source confirming the precise
          genealogical definition.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the exact relationship requires dictionary-level verification.

heading: QUDA

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Quda refers to a person connected to another family through the marriage of their children.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Құда
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Quda
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /qʊˈdɑ/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Құда болу — to become related through marriage; құдалар — the two families or their
          representatives connected through a marriage; құда түсу — the formal process of seeking a marriage alliance.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Quda refers to a person connected to another family through the marriage of their children.

For example, the father of a bride and the father of a groom may address one another as quda. The term can also be used
more broadly for the relationship between the families connected through the marriage.

It is not simply a synonym for father-in-law: it describes a relationship between the families of two people who marry.
sections.Cultural context:
Marriage in traditional Kazakh society could establish relationships not only between two individuals but also between their
families. These relationships were recognised through the concept of quda and the wider institution of qudalyq.
 The relationship could involve formal visits, exchanges, gifts, shared ceremonies and ongoing social interaction.

The exact customs varied according to region, historical period, family circumstances and the form of marriage. Modern families
may maintain some practices while changing or omitting others.
sections.Social function:
●​   Establishes a recognised relationship between two families.
     ●​   Creates connections beyond the married couple.
     ●​   Provides a framework for interaction between the families.
     ●​   Supports cooperation during wedding and family events.
     ●​   Can extend relationships across generations.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Family alliance.
     ●​   Mutual respect.
     ●​   Cooperation.
     ●​   Social continuity.
     ●​   Recognition of marriage as a relationship between families.

The concept should not imply that every marriage is arranged by families or that the couple has no individual agency.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Құдам — my quda.
     ●​   Құда болу — to become related through one's children's marriage.
     ●​   Құдалар келді — the relatives connected through the marriage have arrived.
     ●​   Құда түсу — to formally approach a family regarding marriage.

Example: After two families' children marry, the parents may address one another as quda and maintain a relationship through
family gatherings and visits.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Co-parent-in-law: Sometimes used to describe the relationship between the parents of a married couple, but not
          widely understood.
     ●​   Parents-in-law of the married couple: Clear, though longer than the Kazakh term.
     ●​   Marriage-linked relative: Broad and descriptive.
     ●​   In-law: Too general and may refer to a different relationship.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Quda describes a relationship created when two families become connected through the marriage of their children. For
example, the parents of a bride and the parents of a groom may become quda to one another.

This is different from the English expression father-in-law, which usually describes a person's relationship with their spouse's
father. Quda refers to the relationship between the families themselves.

The concept reflects a broader understanding of marriage in which the union can establish continuing social relationships
between two extended families. These relationships may be maintained through visits, celebrations, mutual respect and
cooperation.

For an international reader, quda can be understood as a relative by marriage, especially a parent of one's child's spouse or a
member of the family connected through the marriage.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Supports: General context of family traditions and marriage-related social customs.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic study of quda and qudalyq, including forms of address and
          the relationships between the families.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the central relationship is clear, but exact terminology and customary details require further
          verification.

heading: QUDALYQ

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Qudalyq refers to the relationship, customary process and social arrangements through which two families become connected by the marriage of their children.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Құдалық
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Qudalyq
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /qʊdɑˈlɯq/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Құда — a relative connected through marriage; құда түсу — to formally approach a family regarding
          marriage; құдалыққа бару — to attend a formal meeting between the families.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Qudalyq refers to the relationship, customary process and social arrangements through which two families become connected
by the marriage of their children.

It can describe the formal interaction between the families before a wedding as well as the continuing relationship established
through the marriage.

The word is derived from quda, referring to a person connected to another family through marriage.
sections.Cultural context:
In traditional Kazakh society, marriage could establish a relationship between two extended families, not only between the bride
and groom.

Qudalyq could involve formal visits, discussions between families, agreements, gifts and ceremonial exchanges. These
interactions helped establish mutual recognition and expectations between the families.

The details of qudalyq varied across regions and historical periods. Contemporary families may preserve selected customs
while adapting the process to modern expectations and individual choices.
sections.Social function:
●​   Establishes a recognised relationship between two families.
     ●​   Provides a framework for discussing and preparing a marriage.
     ●​   Creates opportunities for cooperation and mutual respect.
     ●​   Connects extended family networks.
     ●​   Supports relationships that continue after the wedding.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Family alliance.
     ●​   Mutual respect.
     ●​   Cooperation.
      ●​   Commitment.
     ●​   Social continuity.

The concept should not be presented as proof that all traditional marriages were arranged or that family agreement always
replaced the consent of the couple.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Құдалық жасау — to hold or conduct the customary family process of becoming quda.
     ●​   Құдалыққа бару — to visit the other family as part of the marriage arrangements.
     ●​   Құдалық келісу — to reach an agreement between the families.
     ●​   Құдалық рәсімі — a customary ceremony or gathering connecting the families.

Example: Before a wedding, representatives of the two families visit one another, discuss the arrangements and establish a
formal relationship.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Marriage alliance: Captures the broader relationship between families.
     ●​   Formal family engagement: Useful for describing the process before marriage, but may suggest a Western
          engagement ceremony.
     ●​   Marriage-related family negotiations: Describes one practical aspect.
     ●​   Customary alliance between families: The most useful explanatory equivalent.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Qudalyq is the customary process and relationship through which two families become connected by the marriage of their
children. In traditional settings, marriage could involve formal communication between the families, visits, discussions and
exchanges of gifts.

The process was not limited to organising the wedding. It could establish a relationship that continued long after the ceremony,
creating new connections between extended family networks.

For example, the parents of a prospective bride and groom may meet, discuss the marriage and participate in customary
arrangements. Through this process, the families become quda to one another.

For an international reader, qudalyq is best understood as a traditional process of establishing and maintaining a family alliance
through marriage. Its contemporary forms can differ considerably between families.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Supports: General context of marriage traditions and family relationships.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated ethnographic study of qudalyq, including its stages, regional differences
          and contemporary transformations.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the broad description requires more specific source verification.

heading: QUDAǴY

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Qudaǵy refers to a woman connected to another family through the marriage of their children.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Құдағи
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Qudaǵy
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /qʊdɑˈʁɯ/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Құда — a male relative connected through marriage; құдалар — families connected through
          marriage; құдағи болу — to become related through one's children's marriage.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Qudaǵy refers to a woman connected to another family through the marriage of their children.

A typical example is the mother of the bride in relation to the mother of the groom, or the women representing the two families
in a marriage alliance.

The term is related to quda, but identifies the female form of this marriage-based relationship.
sections.Cultural context:
The term belongs to the vocabulary of qudalyq, the relationship established between families through marriage.

Women from the two families may play important roles in communication, preparation, hospitality and ceremonial activities
surrounding a wedding. In some contexts, the relationship between the two qudaǵy can continue through visits and family
celebrations.

However, the specific responsibilities of women in marriage-related customs have varied across time and communities. The
term itself identifies a relationship, not a universal set of duties.
sections.Social function:
●​   Identifies a woman connected to another family through marriage.
     ●​   Provides a form of address and recognition between families.
     ●​   Helps maintain relationships after a wedding.
     ●​   Supports communication during family occasions.
     ●​   Preserves distinctions in marriage-related kinship vocabulary.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Respect between families.
     ●​   Family alliance.
     ●​   Hospitality.
     ●​   Cooperation.
     ●​   Intergenerational relationships.

The term should not be interpreted as a formal rank or as evidence that all women connected through marriage have the same
social responsibilities.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Құдағиым — my qudaǵy.
     ●​   Құдағи келді — the female relative connected through the marriage has arrived.
     ●​   Құдағилар кездесті — the women connected through the marriage met.

Example: After their children marry, the mothers of the bride and groom maintain contact and address one another as qudaǵy.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Female co-parent-in-law: Descriptive, though unfamiliar to many English speakers.
     ●​   Mother of one's child's spouse: Accurate when referring specifically to the mothers.
     ●​   Female relative by marriage: Broader, but less precise.
     ●​   In-law: Too general to communicate the exact relationship.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Qudaǵy is a Kazakh term for a woman whose family becomes connected to another through the marriage of their children. A
common example is the relationship between the mother of a bride and the mother of a groom.

English does not have a widely used single word for this exact relationship. People would usually explain it by saying the
mother of my child's spouse or my child's spouse's mother.

The term is significant because Kazakh kinship vocabulary distinguishes relationships that English often groups under the
broad category of in-laws. It also reflects the wider social relationship established between two families through marriage.

For an international reader, qudaǵy can be explained as a woman connected to another family through the marriage of their
children, especially the mother of one's child's spouse.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Supports: General context of family relationships and marriage traditions.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated linguistic or ethnographic source confirming the precise use of qudaǵy and
          its relationship to quda.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the definition requires specialist kinship terminology verification.

heading: ABYSYN

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Abysyn refers to a woman whose husband is the brother of another woman's husband.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Абысын
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Abysyn
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ɑbɯˈsɯn/
     ●​   Word class: Noun
     ●​   Related forms: Абысындар — women related through their husbands being brothers; абысын-ажын — a collective
          expression referring to women in this relationship or related female family connections.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Abysyn refers to a woman whose husband is the brother of another woman's husband.

For example, two women married to two brothers are abysyn to one another.

The term identifies a relationship created through marriage and the husbands' sibling relationship. It is not simply a synonym for
sister-in-law in every possible context.
sections.Cultural context:
The term reflects the detailed structure of Kazakh kinship vocabulary and the importance of extended household relationships.

In traditional settings, women married to brothers could share household responsibilities, participate in family events and
maintain relationships within the wider family. Their interactions could involve cooperation as well as disagreement, as in any
close family relationship.

The term should not be romanticised as automatically implying friendship or harmony. It describes a specific relationship, not
the quality of that relationship.
sections.Social function:
●​   Identifies women connected through their husbands' sibling relationship.
     ●​   Helps distinguish particular in-law relationships.
     ●​   Provides a framework for describing extended family interactions.
      ●​   Preserves precise marriage-based kinship terminology.
     ●​   Reflects relationships within interconnected households.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Family cooperation.
     ●​   Shared responsibility.
     ●​   Extended household relationships.
     ●​   Mutual support.
     ●​   Kinship continuity.

The concept should not be used to assume that all abysyn live together or perform the same household roles.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Абысындар — women married to brothers.
     ●​   Абысындар тату — the women related through their husbands are on good terms.
     ●​   Абысынмен араласу — to maintain a relationship with one's abysyn.

Example: Two brothers are married to two women. The women are abysyn to one another.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Sisters-in-law: The closest everyday English equivalent, but it is ambiguous.
     ●​   Wives of brothers: The clearest literal explanation.
     ●​   Women married to brothers: Precise and accessible.
     ●​   Co-sisters-in-law: Sometimes used in anthropological or specialised writing, but unfamiliar to many readers.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Abysyn describes the relationship between two women who are married to brothers. If two brothers each have a wife, those
wives are abysyn to one another.

English generally uses sisters-in-law for several different relationships, including a spouse's sister or a sibling's wife. Kazakh
distinguishes this particular relationship through a separate term.

The term can be important when describing extended family interactions, especially in settings where brothers and their
households remain closely connected. However, the word itself does not mean that the women are necessarily close friends or
share one household.

For an international reader, abysyn is best explained as a woman whose husband is the brother of another woman's husband.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: Broader linguistic and cultural context of Kazakh kinship concepts.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: An authoritative kinship dictionary or ethnographic source confirming the precise
          relationship and any historical household customs associated with it.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the kinship definition should be checked against a specialist source.

heading: QAIYN JURT

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Qaiyn jurt refers to a person's relatives by marriage, particularly the family of their spouse.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Қайын жұрт
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Qaiyn jurt
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /qɑˈjɯn ʒʊɾt/
     ●​   Word class: Noun phrase
     ●​   Related forms: Қайын ата — father-in-law; қайын ене — mother-in-law; қайын аға — husband's or wife's older
          brother, depending on the speaker and context; қайын сіңлі — husband's younger sister, from a woman's
          perspective.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Qaiyn jurt refers to a person's relatives by marriage, particularly the family of their spouse.

It is a collective kinship expression rather than the name of one particular relative. The exact individuals included depend on the
speaker's marital relationship and the context.

The term is related to the wider vocabulary of in-law relationships in Kazakh.
sections.Cultural context:
Marriage creates connections between individuals and their spouse's relatives. Kazakh kinship vocabulary contains specific
terms for different relationships within this network.

The concept of qaiyn jurt provides a collective way to refer to one's in-laws. These relationships may involve visits, family
gatherings, mutual assistance and customary forms of respect.

It is important to distinguish qaiyn jurt from quda: qaiyn jurt refers to one's spouse's relatives, while quda describes the
relationship between families connected through the marriage of their children.
sections.Social function:
●​   Identifies the wider network of relatives connected through marriage.
     ●​   Helps organise social relationships after marriage.
     ●​   Provides a framework for family visits and communication.
     ●​   Supports relationships between spouses and their extended families.
     ●​   Preserves distinctions within kinship vocabulary.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Respect.
     ●​   Family integration.
     ●​   Mutual responsibility.
     ●​   Cooperation.
     ●​   Continuity between families.

The term does not automatically imply closeness or conflict. It identifies a relationship network, while the quality of individual
relationships varies.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Қайын жұртына бару — to visit one's in-laws.
     ●​   Қайын жұртым — my spouse's family.
     ●​   Қайын атам — my father-in-law.
     ●​   Қайын енем — my mother-in-law.

Example: A married person visits their spouse's parents and other relatives during a family celebration.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   In-laws: The most practical general equivalent.
     ●​   Spouse's family: The clearest explanatory translation.
     ●​   Relatives by marriage: More formal and broader.
     ●​   Extended in-law family: Useful when emphasising the wider network.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Qaiyn jurt refers to the family and relatives of one's spouse. After marriage, a person becomes connected not only to their
husband or wife but also to a wider network of relatives, including parents, siblings and other family members.

The term is collective: it does not identify one specific person. English generally uses in-laws or my spouse's family to express
the same idea.

The concept is important because Kazakh vocabulary distinguishes the spouse's family from other kinship groups. It should not
be confused with quda, which describes the relationship between the two families whose children marry.

For an international reader, qaiyn jurt can be understood as the extended family of one's spouse, or one's relatives by marriage.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Supports: General context of Kazakh family and marriage-related relationships.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A specialist dictionary confirming the full range of qaiyn jurt and its related terms.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the broad meaning is clear, but the exact scope should be checked against a kinship
          dictionary.

heading: ATA-BABA

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Ata-baba refers collectively to one's ancestors or forebears.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Ата-баба
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Ata-baba
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ɑˌtɑ bɑˈbɑ/
     ●​   Word class: Noun; collective kinship expression
     ●​   Related forms: Ата-бабалар — ancestors; ата-баба тарихы — ancestral history; ата-баба жолы — the way or
          traditions of one's ancestors.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Ata-baba refers collectively to one's ancestors or forebears.

The expression can include several generations of people from whom a family or community descends. It is used when
discussing genealogy, family history, inherited customs and respect for earlier generations.

Depending on context, it can refer to personal family ancestors or ancestors of a wider community.
sections.Cultural context:
Respect for ancestors and knowledge of family history have an important place in Kazakh cultural discourse. Oral genealogies,
family narratives and shezhire have helped preserve information about earlier generations.

The expression ata-baba appears in discussions of tradition, historical memory and the transmission of cultural practices.
 However, references to ancestors should not be treated as evidence that all customs have remained unchanged. Traditions can
be reinterpreted, adapted or discontinued over time.
sections.Social function:
●​   Preserves family and community history.
     ●​   Connects living generations with earlier generations.
     ●​   Provides a basis for genealogical identity.
     ●​   Supports the transmission of stories and customs.
     ●​   Expresses respect for those who came before.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Respect for ancestors.
     ●​   Historical memory.
     ●​   Family continuity.
     ●​   Gratitude.
     ●​   Intergenerational responsibility.

The concept should not be interpreted as requiring unquestioning acceptance of every practice attributed to the past.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Ата-бабаны құрметтеу — to respect one's ancestors.
     ●​   Ата-баба тарихы — ancestral history.
     ●​   Ата-баба дәстүрі — ancestral tradition.
     ●​   Ата-баба жолын жалғастыру — to continue the traditions or path of one's ancestors.

Example: During a family gathering, an elder tells younger relatives stories about their ancestors and the history of the family.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Ancestors: The most direct and natural equivalent.
     ●​   Forefathers: Appropriate in some contexts, but can sound male-specific.
     ●​   Forebears: A formal and gender-neutral alternative.
     ●​   Previous generations: Useful when discussing generational continuity rather than genealogy.
     ●​   Ancestors and forebears: A broader explanatory phrase.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Ata-baba refers to the ancestors of a family or community. The expression connects people living today with earlier generations
and is commonly used when discussing family history, genealogy and inherited traditions.

For example, an older relative may tell younger family members about their ata-baba, explaining where the family came from,
what earlier generations experienced and which traditions have been passed down.

The concept is not limited to biological descent. In cultural discussion, it can also express respect for historical memory and the
contribution of previous generations.

For an international reader, ata-baba is best understood as one's ancestors or forebears, considered as a collective source of
family history and inherited cultural memory.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
      ●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Supports: General cultural context of ancestry, family traditions and historical continuity.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated linguistic source on the phrase's semantic range and its use in oral
          genealogical narratives.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; general meaning is clear, but specific cultural claims need direct textual support.

heading: URPAQ SABақTASTYǴY

category.title: Family, Kinship and Generational Continuity
category.description: Kinship, ancestry and relationships between generations.

short: Urpaq sabaqtastyǵy means generational continuity: the transmission of knowledge, values, traditions, experiences and responsibilities from one generation to another.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Ұрпақ сабақтастығы
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Urpaq sabaqtastyǵy
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ʊɾˈpɑq sɑbɑqtɑsˈtɯʁɯ/
     ●​   Word class: Noun phrase
     ●​   Related forms: Ұрпақ — generation or descendants; сабақтастық — continuity; ұрпақтар арасындағы байланыс —
          connection between generations; ұрпақтан ұрпаққа — from generation to generation.
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Urpaq sabaqtastyǵy means generational continuity: the transmission of knowledge, values, traditions, experiences and
responsibilities from one generation to another.

The expression combines urpaq (generation or descendants) and sabaqtastyq (continuity or succession).

It can refer to continuity within a family, a community or a wider society.
sections.Cultural context:
The transmission of family history, oral traditions, customs and practical knowledge has been important in Kazakh cultural life.

Older generations may pass on genealogical information, language, stories, traditional skills and social expectations to younger
people. This process can take place within households, through community practices, education and cultural events.

Generational continuity does not mean that traditions remain unchanged. Younger generations may reinterpret, adapt or
selectively preserve what they inherit.
sections.Social function:
●​   Transmits knowledge and cultural practices.
     ●​   Maintains family and community memory.
     ●​   Connects older and younger generations.
     ●​   Supports continuity of language and traditions.
     ●​   Allows societies to preserve and adapt inherited knowledge.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include:

     ●​   Continuity.
     ●​   Respect between generations.
     ●​   Cultural memory.
     ●​   Responsibility.
     ●​   Education and transmission.
     ●​   Connection between past, present and future.

The concept should not be used to suggest that younger generations must accept every inherited belief or custom without
question. Continuity can include adaptation and critical reflection.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Ұрпақ сабақтастығын сақтау — to preserve generational continuity.
     ●​   Ұрпақтан ұрпаққа жеткізу — to pass something from one generation to another.
     ●​   Ұрпақтар сабақтастығы — continuity between generations.
     ●​   Отбасындағы ұрпақ сабақтастығы — generational continuity within a family.

Example: Grandparents teach their grandchildren family history, traditional songs and cultural practices, while the younger
generation adapts some of these traditions to contemporary life.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Generational continuity: The most direct and suitable equivalent.
     ●​   Intergenerational continuity: More academic and formal.
     ●​   Transmission between generations: Emphasises the process of passing on knowledge and practices.
     ●​   Continuity across generations: Clear and accessible.
     ●​   Cultural transmission: Appropriate when the emphasis is specifically on passing down cultural knowledge.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Urpaq sabaqtastyǵy refers to the connection between generations through the transmission of knowledge, values, experiences
and traditions. It describes how a family or society maintains links between its past, present and future.

In a family, this may involve grandparents sharing stories, parents teaching children a language or custom, and younger people
continuing certain practices in their own way. The process is not limited to preserving old traditions exactly as they were. It can
also involve adapting inherited practices to new circumstances.

For an international reader, the concept can be understood as the continuity of knowledge, values and cultural practices
through their transmission from one generation to the next.

Its important feature is the relationship between generations: the past is not simply remembered but contributes to how the
present generation understands itself and how it shapes the future.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” PDF
     ●​   Smagulova, G. N., & Makataeva, Sh. M. (2020). “Лингвоаксиология: қазақтар дүниетанымындағы құндылықтар
          ұғымы.” Eurasian Journal of Philology: Science and Education, 177(1), 187–193. Article
     ●​   Supports: General context of cultural values, traditions and their role in society.
     ●​   Additional evidence needed: A dedicated study of intergenerational transmission in Kazakh families, including
          language, oral history and customary practices.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft; the general concept is clear, but its specifically Kazakh cultural interpretation needs more
          direct evidence.

IV. Traditions, Rituals, and Life-Cycle
Practices — 51–70
Below are all 20 entries in English, following the nine-part structure. They are written for an international audience and designed
to serve as the research content behind your physical cards.

Research note: These are academically oriented draft entries, not twenty fully verified ethnographic studies. I distinguish
established general descriptions from details that still require term-specific evidence. I will not invent page numbers or pretend
that a broad source proves every detail. In particular, some practices vary by region, family, generation, and religious
interpretation.
 Transliteration policy: I use a consistent practical Latin spelling for readability. It is a project convention, not a claim that every
spelling below is the sole officially accepted Kazakh Latin form. The Kazakh Cyrillic headword remains the primary reference.

heading: Túsaukeser

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Túsaukeser literally refers to the cutting of a child's symbolic leg restraints.

sections.Identification:
●​    Kazakh: Тұсаукесер
     ●​    Latin transliteration: Túsaukeser
     ●​    Pronunciation (IPA): /tʊsɑʊ̯kʲesʲer/
     ●​    Word class: Noun; name of a traditional ceremony.
     ●​    Related forms: Тұсау (túsau, a hobble or binding); кесу (kesu, to cut); тұсауын кесу (túsauyn kesu, to cut a child's
           symbolic bonds).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Túsaukeser literally refers to the cutting of a child's symbolic leg restraints. The word combines túsau (a hobble or binding) and
keser (a form associated with cutting). It names a ceremony traditionally performed when a young child begins to walk.
sections.Cultural context:
In the ceremony, a child's legs are symbolically tied, traditionally with a specially prepared cord, and then cut by a selected
person. The act represents the child's transition towards independent movement. The materials and accompanying customs
may vary. Explanations of the ceremony should not assume that every family uses the same cord or follows one fixed
sequence.
sections.Social function:
The ceremony brings relatives and community members together to recognise a child's developmental milestone. It also gives
an honoured participant a role in expressing hopes for the child's future.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include growth, independence, good fortune, and a successful beginning. The person selected to cut the
cord may be expected to represent qualities that the family wishes the child to develop. This is a symbolic expectation, not a
guarantee that the child will acquire those qualities.
sections.Practical application:
●​    Баланың тұсауын кесу — to perform the child's tusaukeser ceremony.
     ●​    Тұсаукесер тойы — a celebration held for the ceremony.
     ●​    Тұсаукесерге шақыру — to invite someone to a tusaukeser.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​    First-steps ceremony: Clear and accessible to international readers.
     ●​    Ceremony of cutting a child's symbolic bonds: More descriptive and culturally informative.
     ●​    Toddler's walking ceremony: Understandable, but less precise.
     ●​    Tusaukeser: Best as the main cultural term, followed by an explanation.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Túsaukeser is a Kazakh ceremony traditionally held when a child begins to walk. A cord is tied around the child's legs and then
cut by a person selected by the family. This action symbolises the removal of obstacles and the beginning of independent
movement. The ceremony is often accompanied by family celebrations and good wishes for the child's future. For an
 international audience, it is important to understand that the cord is symbolic: the ritual is not simply a practical way to teach a
child to walk. It expresses a family's hopes for the child's development and future path.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Vestnik of Novosibirsk State University. Series: History and Philology. Source
     ●​   Zhumadil, A. “The Continuity of Kazakh Rituals and Traditions with Ancient Tribes of Kazakhstan.” Article record
     ●​   Supports: General context for Kazakh ritual practices and their changing role.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A dedicated ethnographic or folkloristic source describing the exact tusaukeser procedure,
          cord types, and regional variation is still required.

heading: Besikke salu

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Besikke salu literally means “placing [a baby] into the besik.” The phrase combines besik, a traditional Kazakh cradle, with salu, meaning “to put” or “to place.” It refers to a ceremony associated with placing an infant in the cradle for t

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Бесікке салу
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Besikke salu
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /bʲesʲikʲːe sɑˈlʊ/
     ●​   Word class: Verbal phrase; name of a traditional infant-care ceremony.
     ●​   Related forms: Бесік (besik, traditional cradle); бесікке бөлеу (besikke böleu, to swaddle or place a baby in a cradle).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Besikke salu literally means “placing [a baby] into the besik.” The phrase combines besik, a traditional Kazakh cradle, with salu,
meaning “to put” or “to place.” It refers to a ceremony associated with placing an infant in the cradle for the first time.
sections.Cultural context:
The besik is a traditional cradle designed for infant care. The ceremony may involve an experienced older woman, family
members, blessings, and customary symbolic actions. Specific procedures differ between families and local traditions. The
cradle itself is an important part of the material culture associated with early childhood.
sections.Social function:
The practice introduces the child to a traditional form of infant care and brings relatives together around the newborn. It can
also recognise the knowledge and experience of older family members.
sections.Cultural values:
The ceremony may express care, protection, continuity between generations, and respect for inherited knowledge. It should not
be presented as proof that all Kazakh families use traditional cradles today.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Баланы бесікке салу — to place a baby in a traditional cradle.
     ●​   Бесік той — a celebration associated with the cradle ceremony.
     ●​   Бесік жыры — cradle song or lullaby.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Cradle ceremony: Concise and appropriate for a card.
     ●​   Traditional cradle ritual: Emphasises the cultural practice.
     ●​   First placement in the cradle: Most literal, but does not communicate the social significance.
     ●​   Besikke salu: Retain the original term when discussing the Kazakh tradition.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Besikke salu is a traditional Kazakh ceremony connected with placing a baby in a besik, a specially designed cradle. It is not
merely the act of putting an infant to sleep. The event can involve experienced relatives, especially older women, and may
include blessings and symbolic customs. The ceremony connects practical childcare with family identity and the transmission of
knowledge between generations. Today, families may preserve the ceremony even if they do not use a traditional cradle in
everyday life.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Zhumadil, A. “The Continuity of Kazakh Rituals and Traditions with Ancient Tribes of Kazakhstan.” Article record
     ●​   Supports: General discussion of Kazakh customs and the continuity and transformation of ritual practices.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A specialised ethnographic source on the besik, its construction, use, and ceremony is
          needed for a fully verified entry.

heading: Shildekhana

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Shildekhana refers to a celebration held after the birth of a child.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Шілдехана
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Shildekhana
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ʃɪlʲdʲeˈχɑnɑ/
     ●​   Word class: Noun; name of a birth-related celebration.
     ●​   Related forms: Шілде (shilde, historically associated with a period of forty days in some Central Asian cultural
          contexts); шілдехана жасау (shildekhana jasau, to hold a shildekhana).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Shildekhana refers to a celebration held after the birth of a child. It is associated with welcoming the newborn and sharing the
news of the birth with relatives and the community.
sections.Cultural context:
The celebration traditionally takes place soon after childbirth. Family members and guests gather to congratulate the parents
and celebrate the arrival of the baby. The timing, scale, and activities vary. It should be distinguished from qyrqynan shyǵaru, a
separate practice associated with the child's first forty days.
sections.Social function:
Shildekhana publicly recognises a new birth and strengthens relationships between the newborn's family and their wider social
circle. It gives relatives an opportunity to offer congratulations and support.
sections.Cultural values:
The practice may express joy, family continuity, hospitality, and collective recognition of a new life. It should not be reduced to a
party: its cultural meaning also comes from the social act of welcoming the child.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Шілдехана жасау — to hold a shildekhana.
     ●​   Шілдеханаға шақыру — to invite someone to the celebration.
     ●​   Шілдехана тойы — a celebration marking a child's birth.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Newborn celebration: Clear and concise.
     ●​   Birth celebration: Broad and accessible.
     ●​   Welcoming-the-baby gathering: Explains its social purpose.
     ●​   Shildekhana: Best retained as the cultural term.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Shildekhana is a traditional Kazakh celebration held after a child is born. Relatives and guests gather to welcome the newborn,
congratulate the parents, and share their happiness. The celebration is part of the wider network of customs surrounding birth
and early childhood. It is important not to confuse it with the forty-day ceremony: shildekhana welcomes the newborn, while
qyrqynan shyǵaru marks a later stage in the child's early life. Modern families may celebrate shildekhana in different ways, from
a small family gathering to a larger event.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Zhumadil, A. “The Continuity of Kazakh Rituals and Traditions with Ancient Tribes of Kazakhstan.” Article record
     ●​   Supports: General background on Kazakh customs and life-cycle traditions.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A source specifically documenting shildekhana and its historical forms is still needed.

heading: Qyrqynan shyǵaru

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Qyrqynan shyǵaru literally means “to bring [the child] out of the forty-day period.” It refers to a traditional ceremony held when a newborn reaches approximately forty days of life.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Қырқынан шығару
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Qyrqynan shyǵaru
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /qɯrqɯˈnɑn ʃɯˈʁɑrʊ/
     ●​   Word class: Verbal phrase; name of an infant-related ritual.
     ●​   Related forms: Қырық күн (qyryq kún, forty days); қырқынан шығару рәсімі (qyrqynan shyǵaru rásimi, the forty-day
          ceremony).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Qyrqynan shyǵaru literally means “to bring [the child] out of the forty-day period.” It refers to a traditional ceremony held when a
newborn reaches approximately forty days of life.
sections.Cultural context:
The ceremony marks the end of an important early period in the child's life. In some versions, the child is bathed using water
into which a number of small objects or coins may be placed. The exact number, objects, sequence, and interpretation can vary.
The practice should be described as a cultural ritual, not as a universal medical requirement.
sections.Social function:
The ceremony marks a transition in the child's early life and brings family members together. It can also provide an occasion for
older relatives to share customary knowledge.
sections.Cultural values:
The practice may express protection, care, renewal, and the importance of early childhood. Its symbolic elements should be
explained without presenting traditional beliefs as scientifically established health claims.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Баланы қырқынан шығару — to perform the forty-day ceremony for a baby.
     ●​   Қырқынан шығару тойы — a celebration marking the ceremony.
     ●​   Қырық күн толу — to reach forty days.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Forty-day baby ceremony: Direct and understandable.
     ●​   Fortieth-day ritual: Concise, but may suggest that the ceremony always occurs exactly on day forty.
     ●​   End-of-the-first-forty-days ceremony: Explains the transition.
     ●​   Qyrqynan shyǵaru: Best retained in a detailed cultural explanation.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Qyrqynan shyǵaru is a traditional Kazakh ceremony associated with a baby's first forty days. It symbolically marks the end of an
early period of vulnerability and the beginning of another stage of infancy. Depending on the family and region, the ceremony
may involve bathing the child and using water prepared with symbolic objects. It is often accompanied by family participation
and good wishes. The number forty has significance in several cultural and religious traditions, so it would be inaccurate to
claim that the practice is exclusively Kazakh or to assign it one universal origin.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Zhumadil, A. “The Continuity of Kazakh Rituals and Traditions with Ancient Tribes of Kazakhstan.” Article record
     ●​   Supports: General background on Kazakh rituals and their historical interpretation.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A direct ethnographic source on the forty-day ceremony and its regional variations is
          required.

heading: At qoyu

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: At qoyu literally means “to give a name.” It refers to the act of naming a person, particularly a newborn child.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Ат қою
     ●​   Latin transliteration: At qoyu
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /ɑt qɔˈjʊ/
     ●​   Word class: Verbal phrase; naming practice.
     ●​   Related forms: Есім (esim, name); есім беру (esim beru, to give a name); ат қою рәсімі (at qoyu rásimi, naming
          ceremony).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
At qoyu literally means “to give a name.” It refers to the act of naming a person, particularly a newborn child. In a cultural
context, it can also refer to the family ceremony or custom surrounding the choice and announcement of a name.
sections.Cultural context:
Kazakh names may reflect family history, religious beliefs, admired qualities, historical figures, nature, or the circumstances
surrounding a child's birth. In some families, an older relative or respected person is invited to name the child. Naming practices
have changed over time and are not governed by one universal traditional procedure.
sections.Social function:
Naming identifies the child as an individual and introduces them into family and social life. The choice can also express family
continuity, respect for elders, and hopes for the child's future.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include identity, memory, aspiration, and belonging. However, the meaning of a name does not
necessarily determine a person's character or future.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Балаға ат қою — to name a child.
     ●​   Ат қою рәсімі — naming ceremony.
     ●​   Есімін кім қойды? — Who gave the child their name?
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Naming: The most natural general equivalent.
     ●​   Naming ceremony: Appropriate when referring to a formal or family event.
     ●​   Name-giving ritual: Emphasises the cultural practice.
     ●​   At qoyu: Useful when discussing the Kazakh custom specifically.
sections.Cultural transfer:
At qoyu is the Kazakh practice of giving a name, especially to a newborn. A name may carry meanings connected with family
memory, religion, history, admired personal qualities, or hopes for the child's future. In some families, a respected elder or
relative is invited to choose the name. The practice is more than the administrative act of registering a birth: it can express how
a family understands identity, belonging, and continuity. However, naming customs differ, and not every Kazakh family follows
the same ceremony or gives the same importance to particular naming traditions.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Supports: General approaches to Kazakh cultural concepts and traditions.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A dedicated study of Kazakh anthroponymy and naming customs is needed for claims about
          name origins, naming authorities, and historical patterns.

heading: Súnnet toi

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Súnnet toi literally means “circumcision celebration.” It refers to a family event held in connection with the circumcision of a boy, a practice associated with Islam.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Сүндет той
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Súnnet toi
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /sʊnˈnʲet tɔj/
     ●​   Word class: Noun phrase; name of a celebration.
     ●​   Related forms: Сүндет (súnnet, circumcision in Islamic usage); сүндетке отырғызу (súnnetke otyrǵyzu, to have a
          boy circumcised); той (toi, celebration or feast).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Súnnet toi literally means “circumcision celebration.” It refers to a family event held in connection with the circumcision of a boy,
a practice associated with Islam.
sections.Cultural context:
Circumcision is an Islamic religious practice and is also part of the cultural life of many Kazakh families. The celebration may
involve relatives, guests, food, gifts, and expressions of congratulations. The age at which it takes place and the scale of the
celebration vary. The medical procedure and the social celebration should be treated as two related but distinct matters.
sections.Social function:
The event brings relatives together and publicly recognises a significant family occasion. It can also express religious and
cultural belonging.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include religious identity, family continuity, community participation, and celebration. It is important not to
imply that every Kazakh family practises or celebrates it in exactly the same way.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Сүндет той жасау — to hold a circumcision celebration.
     ●​   Баланы сүндетке отырғызу — to have a boy circumcised.
     ●​   Сүндет тойға шақыру — to invite someone to a circumcision celebration.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Circumcision celebration: Most direct and accurate.
     ●​   Circumcision feast: Suitable when the meal and gathering are emphasised.
     ●​   Islamic circumcision celebration: Useful when religious context needs to be explicit.
     ●​   Súnnet toi: Retain as the cultural term in a dictionary entry.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Súnnet toi is a Kazakh family celebration connected with the circumcision of a boy. The underlying practice is associated with
Islam and is shared by many Muslim communities beyond Kazakhstan. The celebration may include a family gathering, a meal,
gifts, and congratulations. It is useful to distinguish the religious and medical practice of circumcision from the social event
organised by the family. The term therefore describes not only a procedure but also the way a family may recognise the
occasion within its community.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Gabitkhanuly, K., & Sabyr, M. (2025). “Religious Terminological Concepts – Reflection of Islamic and Traditional
          Kazakh Worldview in Language.” Eurasian Journal of Philology: Science and Education, 199(3), 42–54. Article
     ●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Supports: The interaction of Islamic and Kazakh cultural concepts and the broader context of Kazakh traditions.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A specific ethnographic source on the celebration's historical and contemporary forms is still
          needed.

heading: Tilashar

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Tilashar literally combines til (“language” or “tongue”) and a form of ashu (“to open”).

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Тілашар
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Tilashar
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /tʲɪlɑˈʃɑr/
     ●​   Word class: Noun; name of a traditional educational milestone celebration.
     ●​   Related forms: Тіл (til, language); ашу (ashu, to open); тілашар тойы (tilashar toi, a celebration marking the
          beginning of formal learning).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Tilashar literally combines til (“language” or “tongue”) and a form of ashu (“to open”). In cultural usage, it refers to a celebration
marking a child's beginning of formal education, traditionally associated with learning to read and write.
sections.Cultural context:
The ceremony is associated with a child's first steps into education. In contemporary families, it is often connected with starting
school. It may include a family gathering, gifts, good wishes, and symbolic educational objects. Its exact form varies.
sections.Social function:
Tilashar recognises the transition from early childhood into a more structured educational environment. It allows relatives to
express support for the child's learning and future development.
sections.Cultural values:
The practice may express respect for knowledge, education, literacy, and the child's future. It should not be interpreted as a
uniquely Kazakh celebration of education without comparative evidence.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Тілашар тойы — a tilashar celebration.
     ●​   Балаға тілашар жасау — to hold a tilashar for a child.
     ●​   Тілашарға бата беру — to give a blessing on the occasion of tilashar.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   First-school celebration: Accessible, especially for modern contexts.
     ●​   Literacy initiation ceremony: More precise when the emphasis is learning to read and write.
     ●​   Educational milestone celebration: Broad and suitable for contemporary usage.
     ●​   Tilashar: Best retained as the cultural term.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Tilashar is a Kazakh celebration associated with a child's beginning of education. Traditionally, the idea is connected with
opening the child's path to language and literacy. Today, families may hold it when a child starts school or reaches an important
early educational milestone. The event can include gifts, a family gathering, and blessings for success in learning. It expresses
the importance attached to education and the hopes that relatives have for the child's future. Its form is not fixed and may
change with modern schooling practices.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Supports: General background on Kazakh customs and their adaptation to modern society.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A specialised source documenting the historical development and present-day forms of
          tilashar is required.

heading: Syrǵa salu

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Syrǵa salu literally means “putting on an earring.” In traditional marriage customs, it refers to a ceremony in which an earring is presented to or placed on a woman as a symbolic sign of an agreement between families concerning a future ma

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Сырға салу
      ●​   Latin transliteration: Syrǵa salu
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /sɯrˈʁɑ sɑˈlʊ/
     ●​   Word class: Verbal phrase; name of a marriage-related custom.
     ●​   Related forms: Сырға (syrǵa, earring); сырға тағу (syrǵa taǵu, to wear earrings); құдалық (qudalyq, marriage
          alliance between families).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Syrǵa salu literally means “putting on an earring.” In traditional marriage customs, it refers to a ceremony in which an earring is
presented to or placed on a woman as a symbolic sign of an agreement between families concerning a future marriage.
sections.Cultural context:
The ceremony is associated with the process of establishing a marriage alliance between two families. It may involve
representatives of the prospective groom's family visiting the prospective bride's family, presenting gifts, and discussing the
marriage. The exact procedure and the meaning attached to the earring can vary across regions and generations.
sections.Social function:
Syrǵa salu can formalise communication between families and publicly signal an intention to proceed towards marriage. It may
strengthen relationships between the two families.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include family agreement, commitment, respect, and the formation of new kinship ties. A modern
explanation must also recognise individual consent: a traditional family custom should not be presented as a substitute for the
free consent of the people getting married.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Сырға салу рәсімі — the syrga salu ceremony.
     ●​   Сырға салуға келу — to visit for the syrga salu ceremony.
     ●​   Сырға салынған қыз — a woman for whom the ceremony has been performed.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Engagement ceremony: Convenient, but may suggest a direct equivalent to Western engagement practices.
     ●​   Earring ceremony: Literal but insufficiently explanatory.
     ●​   Marriage-alliance ceremony: Emphasises the relationship between families.
     ●​   Syrǵa salu: Best retained, with a short explanation of its social role.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Syrǵa salu is a Kazakh marriage-related custom in which an earring is presented or placed as a symbolic sign of an agreement
between families concerning a future marriage. The event may include visits, gifts, discussions, and the participation of
relatives. Although it is sometimes translated as an “engagement ceremony,” the two practices should not automatically be
treated as identical. Syrga salu can place particular emphasis on the relationship between families, rather than only on a private
promise between two individuals. Contemporary interpretations vary, and the custom should not be used to imply that family
agreement replaces the consent of the future spouses.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: General background on marriage customs and Kazakh cultural concepts.
      ●​   Verification status: Draft. A dedicated ethnographic study of syrga salu, its regional forms, and its historical changes
          is needed.

heading: Qyz uzatu

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Qyz uzatu literally means “sending off a daughter.” It refers to the ceremony in which a bride is formally seen off from her parental home as she enters married life.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Қыз ұзату
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Qyz uzatu
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /qɯz ʊzɑˈtʊ/
     ●​   Word class: Verbal phrase; name of a marriage ceremony.
     ●​   Related forms: Қыз (qyz, girl or daughter); ұзату (uzatu, to send off or see someone off); ұзатылған қыз (uzatylǵan
          qyz, a daughter who has been married and sent off).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Qyz uzatu literally means “sending off a daughter.” It refers to the ceremony in which a bride is formally seen off from her
parental home as she enters married life.
sections.Cultural context:
The ceremony traditionally involves the bride's family, relatives, guests, and representatives of the groom's side. It may include
speeches, songs, blessings, gifts, and symbolic farewells. In contemporary Kazakhstan, it is often organised as a large wedding
celebration, although its format varies widely.
sections.Social function:
Qyz uzatu marks a major transition in family relationships. It publicly recognises the bride's departure from her parental
household and the creation of a new marriage-based relationship between families.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include family continuity, respect for parents, transition, and the formation of new kinship ties. It should
not be interpreted as meaning that a woman loses her relationship with her birth family after marriage.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Қыз ұзату тойы — a bride's farewell celebration.
     ●​   Қызын ұзату — to see one's daughter off for marriage.
     ●​   Ұзатылып жатқан қыз — a bride being formally seen off by her family.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Bride's farewell ceremony: Communicates the central symbolic action.
     ●​   Wedding send-off: Accessible but somewhat informal.
     ●​   Bride's family ceremony: Emphasises the role of her family.
     ●​   Qyz uzatu: Best retained as the cultural term.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Qyz uzatu is a Kazakh wedding ceremony in which a bride is formally seen off from her parental home. It is often organised by
the bride's family and may include a gathering of relatives, speeches, songs, blessings, and symbolic acts of farewell. The
ceremony represents a transition into married life and the establishment of new relationships between families. It is sometimes
described simply as a wedding, but this misses its particular focus on the bride's family and their role in the transition. The
custom does not mean that the bride stops belonging to her birth family.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: General context of marriage traditions and cultural concepts.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A specialised ethnographic source on the structure and regional forms of qyz uzatu is
          needed.

heading: Kelin túsiru

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Kelin túsiru literally means “bringing in a bride.” It refers to the reception of a bride into her husband's family or household after marriage.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Келін түсіру
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Kelin túsiru
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /kʲelʲin tʊˈsɪrʊ/
     ●​   Word class: Verbal phrase; name of a marriage-related custom.
     ●​   Related forms: Келін (kelin, bride or daughter-in-law); түсіру (túsiru, to bring down, bring in, or receive); келін болып
          түсу (kelin bolyp túsu, to enter a family as a bride).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Kelin túsiru literally means “bringing in a bride.” It refers to the reception of a bride into her husband's family or household after
marriage.
sections.Cultural context:
The custom is connected with the bride's arrival at the groom's family home. Depending on the region and family, it may involve
welcoming rituals, blessings, greetings, and other marriage-related ceremonies. It is often discussed alongside betashar, but
the two terms do not refer to exactly the same action.
sections.Social function:
Kelin túsiru marks the bride's entry into a new family network and provides an occasion for the two families to establish or
strengthen relationships.
sections.Cultural values:
Possible associations include hospitality, family continuity, kinship, and the formation of new social relationships. A modern
account should avoid presenting the bride as someone who simply becomes subordinate to the husband's family; contemporary
family arrangements vary.
sections.Practical application:
●​   Келін түсіру тойы — a celebration welcoming a bride into the groom's family.
     ●​   Келін түсіру дәстүрі — the custom of receiving a bride.
     ●​   Келін болып түсу — to enter a family as a bride.
sections.Translation analysis:
●​   Welcoming the bride into the groom's family: Most explanatory.
     ●​   Bride's reception ceremony: Concise and useful for a card.
     ●​   Bringing home the bride: Literal, but may sound overly informal or imply ownership.
     ●​   Kelin túsiru: Best retained as the cultural term.
sections.Cultural transfer:
Kelin túsiru is the Kazakh custom of receiving a bride into her husband's family after marriage. It marks a change in family
relationships and the beginning of her participation in a new network of relatives. The reception may involve greetings,
blessings, and other customs, depending on the family's regional and personal traditions. It is closely connected with the wider
wedding process, but it should not be treated as identical to betashar, which is a more specific ceremony involving the symbolic
introduction of the bride. The term describes a social transition, not simply physical arrival at a house.
sections.Evidence:
●​   Zhetpysbaev, S. K. (2023). “Traditions and Customs of the Kazakh People: Place and Role in the Modernization of
          Society.” Source
     ●​   Akhmetzhanova, Z. K. (2012). Очерки по национальной концептологии. Repository record
     ●​   Supports: General background on marriage customs and Kazakh cultural concepts.
     ●​   Verification status: Draft. A specific source on the reception of the bride and its regional variations is required.

heading: Betashar

category.title: Traditions, Rituals and Life-Cycle Practices
category.description: Ceremonies and practices marking important moments in life.

short: Betashar literally means “opening the face.” It refers to a wedding ceremony in which the bride is formally introduced to the groom's relatives and the wider family community.

sections.Identification:
●​   Kazakh: Беташар
     ●​   Latin transliteration: Betashar
     ●​   Pronunciation (IPA): /bʲetɑˈʃɑr/
     ●​   Word class: Noun; name of a marriage ceremony.
     ●​   Related forms: Бет (bet, face); ашу (ashu, to open); беташар жыры (betashar jyry, betashar song).
sections.Linguistic meaning:
Betashar literally means “opening the face.” It refers to a wedding ceremony in which the bride is formally introduced to the
groom's relatives and the wider family community.
sections.Cultural context:
